title: Where was Agade, the capital of the Sargonic empire?
short: The city from which Sargon and his successors ruled Mesopotamia c. 2300 BCE has never been securely located, despite more than a century of searching in central Iraq.
matters: Agade was the political centre of the first territorial state in Mesopotamia, and its archives, workshops and temple of Ishtar-Annunitum are presumed to hold the administrative and royal records that the provincial finds only reflect. Without the site, accounts of Sargonic administration, art production and the empire's collapse rest on texts from Nippur, Girsu, Adab and other subordinate centres and on later literary traditions such as the Curse of Agade. Its location also fixes the historical geography of the lower Diyala and Tigris and the route network described in Old Babylonian itineraries.
stuck: No inscription naming Agade has been found in situ, and the textual indications (proximity to Sippar, Kish, Eshnunna and the Tigris, a river crossing in Mari itineraries) are compatible with several regions. The Tigris has shifted course since the third millennium, so sites once on its banks may now lie under alluvium, under modern Baghdad or under later occupation. Fieldwork in central Iraq was interrupted for long periods after 1980, and candidate mounds such as Ishan Mizyad and Tell Mohammed have yielded no Sargonic monumental remains.
solved: A ranked list of candidate sites, each scored against every dated textual reference to Agade's position and against reconstructed third-millennium river courses, followed by excavation or coring at the top candidate that recovers Sargonic remains together with inscriptions naming the city or its temple Eulmash.
approach: The location debate already has a long human literature to build on: the Kish-region case of Weiss (1975), the areal reconstruction of Wall-Romana (1990), Kutscher (1998) on the Diyala approaches, Reade (2002) on monuments and routes, and the reviews of the evidence in Kawakami (2022) and Kawakami (2023). The Sargonic inscriptions in Frayne (1993) and the Old Babylonian dossier gathered by Ziegler (2014) are the textual core.

Teams could compile every attestation of Agade from the third millennium to the Neo-Babylonian period (royal inscriptions, Mari and Eshnunna letters, itineraries, kudurrus, year names) from CDLI, ORACC and ARCHIBAB. Each statement of distance, direction, river crossing or neighbouring town becomes a dated constraint, with assyriologists deciding how literally formulaic or literary references such as Cooper (1983) should be taken.

The landscape side builds on the channel reconstructions in Gasche and Tanret (1998) and the remote-sensing work of Hritz (2010), tracing palaeochannels and mounds on CORONA and other declassified imagery so that textual constraints can be tested against where watercourses actually ran in the late third millennium.

The main rival hypotheses, a site near Kish and Babylon, one on the Tigris near the Diyala confluence, or one further north near Samarra, predict different travel times and river relations in the Mari and Eshnunna letters, so weighting each constraint by its date and reliability shows which zone the texts favour.

Even without a find, the result would be a published probability surface with its assumptions laid out, which narrows survey targets and can be revised as new tablets appear. The answer will remain a region rather than a mound until there is excavated evidence.

Confirmation depends on Iraqi institutions and international field teams: survey, geoarchaeological coring and excavation under the State Board of Antiquities and Heritage, and publication of tablets now held in the Iraq Museum.

title: How many people lived in the Americas in 1492?
short: Estimates of the hemisphere's population on the eve of contact run from about 8 million to over 100 million, and the scale of the collapse depends on which is right.
matters: The contact population sets the scale of the demographic collapse that followed, and so the magnitude of the most consequential mortality event of the early modern world. It underpins arguments about the density and environmental impact of Indigenous societies (including the extent of anthropogenic landscapes in Amazonia and eastern North America), about the labor economies of the Spanish and Portuguese empires, and about whether reforestation of abandoned land contributed to the atmospheric CO2 minimum around 1610 that Lewis and Maslin proposed as a marker for the Anthropocene.
stuck: Almost no direct counts exist for 1492: early colonial tribute lists, visitas and missionary reports begin decades after epidemics had already struck, so every estimate projects backward through assumed depopulation ratios or carrying capacities. Hemispheric totals are built by summing regional estimates of very uneven quality, and the same sparse figures support results as different as Kroeber's roughly 8.4 million and Dobyns's 90–112 million. Archaeological proxies (settlement counts, radiocarbon date densities, LiDAR-mapped house platforms) measure occupation over centuries rather than population at a single date.
solved: A regional-level reconstruction for c. 1492 in which every region's estimate is tied to an openly published dataset of documentary counts and archaeological proxies, with stated assumptions and uncertainty intervals, such that the hemispheric total and its interval can be recomputed and the main regional disagreements (central Mexico, the Andes, Amazonia, eastern North America) are each narrowed by independent lines of evidence.
approach: The estimates span more than an order of magnitude, from the low totals of Kroeber (1939) and Rosenblat (1954) to the high counts built on tribute data by Borah and Cook (1963) and Dobyns (1966). The critiques of Zambardino (1980), Henige (1998) and Livi-Bacci (2003), and the regional syntheses in Denevan (1992), Thornton (1987) and Milner and Chaplin (2010), show where those figures are fragile.

Teams could extract every population figure from digitized tribute rolls, visitas, relaciones geográficas and mission registers into a common table recording date, place, unit counted (tributaries, households, souls) and source. The conversion of tributaries into total population is the decision that most shapes the result, so it should be kept as an explicit, adjustable parameter rather than buried in the figures.

With the table in place, depopulation curves can be fitted province by province instead of assumed. The rival models, an early pandemic collapse preceding Spanish counts versus a slower, staggered decline driven by war, famine and labour regimes, differ in what they predict for the earliest assessments, and cases like the delayed fall documented by Liebmann (2016) in the Jemez region help tell them apart.

Archaeology supplies an independent check: LiDAR surveys such as Canuto (2018) for the Maya lowlands and Prümers (2022) for the Bolivian Amazon, and radiocarbon date densities like those used by Kelly (2025), can yield occupation estimates for the decades just before contact.

An intermediate result would be a set of province-level ranges with documented assumptions, which would already sharpen the inputs used in Earth-system studies such as Koch (2019). Any hemispheric total will remain a wide range, and historians and archaeologists should review how each regional figure was derived.

Much depends on further digitization and transcription of tribute and visita series in the Archivo General de Indias, the Archivo General de la Nación (Mexico), and Andean visitas and revisitas in Lima and Sucre, and on collaboration with archaeologists and Indigenous communities whose lands hold the settlement evidence.

title: When was Beowulf composed?
short: Proposed dates for the poem range from about 700 to the early eleventh century, the date of its only manuscript, and rest on metre, language, palaeography and historical context.
matters: An early date (before about 750) makes Beowulf a witness to the culture of Christian Mercia or Northumbria and to oral-traditional material close to the migration period; a date in the Viking age or the reign of Cnut makes it a product of Anglo-Scandinavian politics and late West Saxon literary culture. The choice shapes readings of the poem's attitude to pagan ancestors, Danish kings and Christianity, and its use as evidence for early English legend, Germanic heroic tradition and the history of Old English verse.
stuck: The poem survives in one manuscript copied around 1000, so internal evidence of composition date must be separated from changes introduced by copying. Metrical tests such as Kaluza's law depend on phonological distinctions whose dating and dialect distribution are themselves inferred, and the corpus of securely dated Old English verse is very small. Arguments from palaeographic error patterns, vocabulary and historical allusion each point to a range rather than a date, and scholars weigh them differently.
solved: A dating model trained on Old English texts with independently established dates and transmission histories that assigns Beowulf a composition interval with calibrated uncertainty, and that correctly recovers the known dates of held-out texts, including texts preserved only in late copies.
approach: The debate is well mapped by human scholarship: the conference volume Chase (1981), the late-date case of Kiernan (1981), the metrical history of Fulk (1992), Lapidge (2000) on letter-form errors in the archetype, the retrospect of Frank (2007), and the essays in Neidorf (2014). Neidorf (2017) argues that scribal modernization can be separated from the poet's own language.

Teams could build a feature set for every Old English poem and dated prose text from the Dictionary of Old English Corpus and manuscript facsimiles: metrical features such as Kaluza's law, contraction and parasite vowels, along with morphology, vocabulary, spelling layers and scribal error types. Which features count as authorial and which as scribal is the decision that shapes everything downstream, and it belongs with philologists.

The quantitative profiling of Neidorf (2019) shows the method can work at scale; a next step would calibrate a model only on texts with independent dating and treat copying as an explicit source of noise, so that it reports which features drive any estimate.

The rival positions, composition around 700 or earlier versus a tenth- or eleventh-century poem close to the manuscript, make different predictions: an early poem should show archaic metrical patterns that scribes failed to update, while a late one should show them only as imitation. Testing those features against Klaeber's edition, Fulk (2008), and the readings in Electronic Beowulf would show which pattern holds.

A shareable annotated corpus of metrical and orthographic features would be useful for other Old English poems even if Beowulf's date stays contested, and the estimate itself will remain a range of decades or centuries rather than a year.

All key witnesses are already digitized, so the main need is careful philological annotation by Old English specialists, along with continued open access to the Dictionary of Old English Corpus and British Library images.

title: Did the Black Death reach sub-Saharan Africa in the fourteenth century?
short: Plague devastated Egypt and North Africa in 1347–49, but whether it crossed the Sahara or reached the Horn and East Africa is unresolved.
matters: If plague reached West, East or Northeast Africa, it would offer an explanation for site abandonments, settlement shifts and political reorganizations that archaeologists date to the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, from the forest zone of southern Ghana to Ife, and it would change how historians read the demographic and political background to the Atlantic encounter. It also bears on the global history of the second pandemic, on whether the Yersinia pestis lineages now endemic in Central and East Africa descend from medieval introductions, and on the long-standing assumption that Africa south of the Sahara was untouched while Eurasia and North Africa lost a large share of their populations.
stuck: Written sources from sub-Saharan Africa for the fourteenth century are few, and Arabic chroniclers who described plague in Egypt and the Maghrib were largely silent about lands beyond the Sahara, a silence that can be read either as absence of plague or absence of reporting. Archaeological signs such as abandonments, mass burials or population decline have other possible causes (drought, war, trade shifts), and few sites are dated precisely enough to tie them to the 1340s–1400s. No medieval Y. pestis genome has yet been published from sub-Saharan Africa, so the genetic argument rests on inferences from the phylogeny of modern African strains.
solved: Recovery of Yersinia pestis DNA, radiocarbon-dated to c. 1340–1500, from human remains at one or more sub-Saharan sites, placed on the second-pandemic phylogeny; or, conversely, systematic negative screening of well-dated fourteenth- and fifteenth-century burials across several regions combined with a full survey of the textual evidence showing no plague references.
approach: Start from the regional work already done: Chouin (2018) on the fourteenth-century abandonment of earthwork settlements in southern Ghana and at Ife, Gallagher (2018) on which archaeological signatures can and cannot distinguish plague from drought or war, Derat (2018) on Ge'ez lexical and talismanic evidence from the Horn, and Green (2018) on what the phylogeny of modern African strains does and does not show. Chapelain de Seréville-Niel (2022) and Chapelain de Seréville-Niel (2024) set out what the already excavated skeletal material from Benin City and Ile-Ife can bear, including a mass grave opened in the early 1960s.

Build from the archaeological literature a geo-referenced register of candidate sites and of human remains, with radiocarbon determinations recorded as calibrated ranges and with the original laboratory codes. The choice that shapes everything after it is whether a candidate is defined by settlement disruption or by dated human remains whose range overlaps c. 1340-1500; these are different classes of evidence and should be kept separate rather than merged into one map of 'plague sites'.

In parallel, compile a dated register of references to epidemic mortality, and of the places and years for which sources are silent, from Arabic and Ge'ez texts, fifteenth-century Portuguese accounts in the Torre do Tombo, and the West African manuscripts imaged from Timbuktu and the Ethiopian collections in the Endangered Archives Programme. Most of these manuscripts are later copies, so each reference needs its witness dated by specialists before it counts as fourteenth-century testimony.

Some progress needs no new excavation: re-screening the published shotgun data from African ancient-DNA studies held in the European Nucleotide Archive, including the medieval Swahili coast individuals sequenced by Brielle (2023), with authentication workflows such as the one described by Pochon (2023), and reporting coverage and detection limits for each individual. Even a set of negatives establishes how many dated burials have now been tested and how deeply.

The two hypotheses can be stated so that evidence separates them. Chouin (2018) and Green (2020) argue for fourteenth-century introductions south of the Sahara, while Mas Fiol (2024), working from a large collection of modern isolates, dates the spread of the 1.ANT lineage into continental Africa to the late seventeenth century and after; a medieval genome from a sub-Saharan burial, placed on the second-pandemic framework of Spyrou (2019), would decide between them, and its absence would not. Until then the honest output is region by region, plague attested, screened without detection, or untested, rather than a single continental verdict.

Everything beyond the computational re-screening depends on institutions: ancient-DNA laboratories, and museums and heritage authorities in Nigeria, Ghana, Tanzania and Ethiopia, which hold both the remains and the excavation records, among them the Kilwa Kisiwani and Aksum field archives of the British Institute in Eastern Africa. Sampling and radiocarbon dating should proceed under protocols agreed with those authorities and with descendant communities, and with African archaeologists and bioarchaeologists reviewing both the registers and any laboratory result.

title: How many people lived in China around 1600, and how many died between 1620 and 1680?
short: Late Ming population estimates run from about 150 million to over 200 million, so the scale of the mid-seventeenth-century collapse remains uncertain by tens of millions.
matters: The size of the late Ming population sets the denominator for comparisons of Chinese and European living standards, urbanization and per capita output, including recent historical national accounts. It also determines how catastrophic the Ming–Qing transition was: whether the wars, epidemics and famines of 1620–1680 killed a few tens of millions or a much larger share of the population, and how far the climate-crisis interpretation of the seventeenth century rests on China. Qing-era growth rates, and therefore arguments about the eighteenth-century population boom, depend on where the seventeenth-century trough lay.
stuck: Official Ming registers record roughly 60 million people throughout the dynasty, a figure that reflects fiscal quotas fixed after 1393 rather than headcounts, so every modern total is a reconstruction. Ho Ping-ti (1959) proposed about 150 million for 1600; later work, including Cao Shuji's prefecture-level reconstruction, puts the late Ming peak close to 200 million, with some estimates higher. The central Yellow Register archive in Nanjing was lost, local gazetteer figures vary in what they count, and corrections for under-registration have been applied region by region with assumptions that are hard to compare.
solved: A county- or prefecture-level population series for c.1580, 1630 and 1680 covering at least the core provinces, in which every adjustment to registered figures is stated as an explicit, reproducible rule, and whose implied densities and trends are shown to be consistent with independent evidence on cultivated land, land clearance, grain prices and tax arrears.
approach: Agents can extract every household, ding and mouth figure, land total and tax quota from the digitized Ming and early Qing gazetteers into a single database keyed to CHGIS county boundaries, recording the year and the registration category of each number.

Historians can then specify alternative under-registration models (for example, by ratio of ding to mouths, or by comparison with 1680s Qing registration) and run them consistently across counties, with the agents flagging outliers and internal contradictions for human review.
Cross-checks against grain-price series, reclamation memorials of the 1650s–1680s and local reports of depopulation would test whether a given model produces plausible regional trajectories.
The surviving Yellow Register fragments reused as book-backing paper could provide household-level calibration points if they are systematically imaged and transcribed.

title: What caused the cocoliztli epidemics of 1545 and 1576 in New Spain?
short: Two epidemics that Nahua and Spanish observers called cocoliztli killed a large share of central Mexico's Indigenous population, and their cause, whether a native haemorrhagic fever, enteric fever or something else, is disputed.
matters: The cocoliztli epidemics of 1545–48 and 1576–80 are counted among the largest mortality events in the sixteenth-century collapse of Mexico's Indigenous population, with contemporary and modern estimates of losses ranging widely and in some accounts exceeding the toll of the 1520 smallpox epidemic. Whether they were caused by a pathogen introduced from Europe or Africa, by a native disease released by drought and colonial disruption, or by several agents together changes how the collapse is explained: as an inevitable consequence of contact, or as the product of colonial labour, resettlement and famine acting on susceptible populations.
stuck: The clinical descriptions (high fever, bleeding from nose and mouth, jaundice, rapid death, Indigenous victims and few Spanish ones) fit several modern diseases, and sixteenth-century terms like cocoliztli ('pestilence') were generic. Rodolfo Acuña-Soto and colleagues proposed a native rodent-borne haemorrhagic fever amplified by drought, but no such virus has been identified, and RNA viruses rarely survive to be detected in skeletal remains. Vågene et al. (2018) recovered Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C from an epidemic cemetery at Teposcolula-Yucundaa, but from one site in the Mixteca Alta and with the acknowledged possibility that other, undetectable pathogens were also present, so the finding has not settled the question for 1545 in central Mexico or for 1576 at all.
solved: Pathogen evidence from several independently dated epidemic burials of 1545–48 and 1576–80, in central Mexico as well as Oaxaca, identifies the same agent or combination of agents, and the agent's known epidemiology is consistent with the timing, symptoms, age and ethnic pattern of mortality, and geography recorded in the Relaciones geográficas, parish and cabildo records.
approach: Build on the demographic and documentary work of Cook (1991), McCaa (1995) and Cook (1998), the haemorrhagic-fever case made by Acuña-Soto (2000) and Marr (2000), and the drought argument of Acuña-Soto (2002). The pictorial annals, read through Mengin (1952), and recent readings of the Florentine Codex by Ríos Castaño (2025) show how much the Nahuatl sources still have to give.

Extract every report of the 1545 and 1576 epidemics from the Relaciones geográficas of 1579–85, Sahagún's writings, Francisco Hernández, Juan de Torquemada, the Codex en Cruz and Codex Mexicanus, viceregal correspondence and the Mexico City cabildo minutes. Each report becomes a record of symptoms, dates, place, mortality claim and who died, with Spanish and Nahuatl testimony kept distinct and the date of writing recorded, since many accounts were set down decades after the events.

A georeferenced, source-graded atlas of the two epidemics would be useful on its own terms, showing where the documentary record is dense, where it is silent, and how far later chroniclers copied one another.

Set the atlas against the gridded soil-moisture reconstructions of Stahle (2016) and against the spread of cattle, wheat, congregación and repartimiento labour. A drought-and-rodent reservoir model, a colonial-disruption model and a contagion-along-routes model predict different geographies and timings of mortality, and the comparison should be reviewed by historians of New Spain before any is preferred.

Treat the pathogen as an open question. The Salmonella Paratyphi C genomes from Teposcolula-Yucundaa reported by Vågene (2018), with the context in Warinner (2012), Zhou (2018) and Bravo-Lopez (2025), establish one infection at one site, not the cause of the whole epidemic; mortality totals, too, will stay a wide range.

Testing that result depends on INAH and palaeogenomic laboratories: identifying securely dated epidemic burials in Mexico City, Puebla, Oaxaca and elsewhere, and screening them with methods able to recover RNA viruses and parasites as well as bacteria, under protocols agreed with descendant communities.

title: How, if at all, did Copernicus learn of the Maragha-school planetary models?
short: Copernicus used devices found earlier in al-Ṭūsī and Ibn al-Shāṭir, but no document shows how a text containing them reached him or his teachers.
matters: If Copernicus drew on the Ṭūsī couple and Ibn al-Shāṭir's lunar and Mercury models, the Copernican revolution sits at the end of a continuous Arabic and Persian reform of Ptolemaic astronomy rather than at a Latin new beginning. The answer bears on how historians describe the relation between Islamic science and the Renaissance, on the role of Byzantine and Jewish intermediaries in fifteenth-century Italy, and on Swerdlow's reconstruction of how Copernicus reached heliocentrism in the first place.
stuck: The mathematical parallels have been clear since Kennedy and Roberts (1959) and Swerdlow and Neugebauer (1984), but Copernicus cites no Arabic author for these devices, and no Latin translation of al-Ṭūsī's Tadhkira or Ibn al-Shāṭir's Nihāyat al-sūl is known. The one securely located carrier, a Ṭūsī-couple diagram in a Byzantine Greek astronomical text in Vat. gr. 211, proves the device reached Italy but not that Copernicus saw it. Skeptics (Di Bono 1995, Blåsjö 2014, 2018) argue that the devices could have been derived independently or from Latin sources such as Proclus, so parallels alone cannot settle the question.
solved: A dated document (a manuscript, annotation, library inventory, loan record or letter) that places a text describing the Ṭūsī couple or Ibn al-Shāṭir's models in the hands of Copernicus, one of his teachers, or a scholar demonstrably in contact with him in Kraków, Bologna, Rome, Padua or Ferrara before about 1514. Alternatively, a documented exhaustive search of the relevant manuscript holdings that finds no such carrier would narrow the hypothesis to independent invention or oral transmission.
approach: Start from the technical and textual work already done: the parallels established by Kennedy (1959) and Swerdlow and Neugebauer (1984), Ragep's (2017) survey of the versions of the Ṭūsī couple in Arabic, Greek, Hebrew and Latin, Nikfahm-Khubravan (2019) on the Mercury models, and Morrison (2025) on intermediaries such as Moses Galeano. Set beside them the objections of Di Bono (1995) and Blåsjö (2014), so that the documentary standard the skeptics ask for is stated before the search begins.

Build a census of every manuscript known to contain the Ṭūsī couple or an Ibn al-Shāṭir-type model, in any language, using ISMI and the Ptolemaeus Arabus et Latinus catalogues as starting points. Each witness should be recorded by the specific device and variant it carries, since a rectilinear couple, a curvilinear one and a full lunar model point to different routes.

Cross-reference provenance, ownership marks, binding evidence and library inventories for these witnesses against a prosopography of Copernicus's teachers in Kraków and Bologna, his Paduan contemporaries such as Amico and Fracastoro, and the Greek and Jewish scholars in contact with them. Agents can draft the links, but specialists in palaeography and codicology should confirm each one.

Short of finding a carrier, a dated map of where each variant of the device is attested in Italy and Central Europe before 1514 would already narrow the question; it can start from Vat. gr. 211 and Bessarion's books in the Marciana. Later Paduan uses, such as the reciprocation mechanism in Luchini's treatise studied by Omodeo (2025), help show which variants were circulating in the region.

Test the rival hypotheses against that map: a Byzantine Greek route, a Hebrew route via texts such as the one discussed by Nosonovsky (2018), oral transmission through Galeano's circle, and independent derivation from Latin sources. If no carrier is found, the outcome will be a documented negative that shifts the weight between these explanations rather than a proof either way.

Progress depends on libraries digitizing and describing uncatalogued Greek and Hebrew astronomical miscellanies in Italian, Polish and Central European collections, including the Jagiellonian Library's fifteenth-century teaching manuscripts, and on curators willing to examine ownership notes and bindings that images alone cannot show.

title: Which lost works of Galen survive unrecognised in Arabic and Syriac?
short: Many Galenic works lost in Greek were translated into Syriac and Arabic in ninth-century Baghdad; some may survive in unedited manuscripts or in quotations not yet traced to their source.
matters: Galen is the largest surviving author of Greek antiquity, yet his own lists and Hunayn ibn Ishaq's Risala name many works whose Greek text is lost, including logical, philosophical and Hippocratic commentaries. Several have already been recovered wholly or partly from Arabic (On Medical Experience, the later books of On Anatomical Procedures, On Examinations by which the Best Physicians are Recognised, the commentaries on Epidemics II and VI), and each recovery has changed accounts of ancient empiricism, anatomy or Hippocratic exegesis. Identifying further texts would also clarify what Arabic medicine and philosophy actually inherited from Galen, as opposed to what later authors attributed to him.
stuck: Hunayn's Risala (c. 863, with later additions) describes about 129 Galenic works translated into Syriac or Arabic, but many of those translations survive only as quotations embedded in later compilations such as al-Razi's al-Hawi, Maimonides' Medical Aphorisms and Ibn Abi Usaybi'a's biographical dictionary, often paraphrased and attributed loosely. Large numbers of Arabic medical manuscripts in Istanbul, Iran, the Escorial and elsewhere remain uncatalogued in detail or unedited, and the Syriac layer, as the Galen Palimpsest shows, often survives only as erased undertext. Matching an Arabic paraphrase to a lost Greek work requires simultaneous command of Galen's Greek corpus, Hunayn's translation vocabulary and the Arabic compilers' citation habits, a combination few scholars have.
solved: A passage or treatise in Arabic or Syriac is shown to derive from a Galenic work lost in Greek, by matching its title and content to Galen's or Hunayn's descriptions, by translation-vocabulary alignment with Hunayn's known versions, and by at least one independent witness (a second manuscript, a Greek or Latin fragment, or an attributed quotation elsewhere).
approach: Build a register of every Galenic work lost or incomplete in Greek, starting from Fichtner's Corpus Galenicum bibliography and Hunayn's Risala as edited by Lamoreaux, with Galen's own descriptions of each work's contents.

Use research agents to align Galen's surviving Greek (Kühn's edition and the Corpus Medicorum Graecorum) with Hunayn-school Arabic translations through the Glossarium Graeco-Arabicum and Ullmann's lexical work, producing a model of how specific Greek terms and phrases were rendered.

Apply that model to machine-readable Arabic compilations in OpenITI (al-Razi's al-Hawi, Ibn Abi Usaybi'a, Maimonides) to flag Galen-attributed passages that match no extant Greek work, and cluster them by likely source title.

Prioritise manuscripts that Sezgin, Ullmann and Fichtner list as unedited Galenic translations and seek imaging and catalogue collaboration with the Süleymaniye Library, Iranian libraries and the Escorial where copies are not yet online.

title: By what route did knowledge of gunpowder reach Latin Europe in the thirteenth century?
short: Gunpowder formulas appear in China by 1044 and in Arabic and Latin texts by the later 1200s, but the path between them is unattested.
matters: The route determines whether gunpowder should be described as a Mongol-era transfer across Eurasia, a product of Mamluk and Andalusian Arabic chemistry, or a partly independent European development from Chinese-derived saltpetre knowledge. It shapes debates over the 'military revolution', over the role of the Mongol empire as a conduit of technology, and over the place of the Islamic world in histories of chemistry and warfare that often move directly from China to Europe.
stuck: The Chinese Wujing zongyao (compiled c. 1040–1044) gives the earliest surviving formulas, but the next datable recipes appear almost simultaneously in the 1260s–1290s in Latin (Roger Bacon's allusions in the Opus maius and Opus tertium, c. 1267; the Liber ignium attributed to Marcus Graecus) and in Arabic (Ḥasan al-Rammāḥ, c. 1270s–1280s), with no text recording a transfer. Arabic terms such as naft and Latin descriptions of incendiaries are ambiguous about whether they mean gunpowder, and the dating of many recipe collections rests on late manuscript copies. Bacon's supposed anagram recipe has been regarded as doubtful since the early twentieth century.
solved: A securely dated text, or a stemma of dated manuscripts, that shows one of the Latin or Arabic gunpowder recipe traditions copying or translating from an identifiable earlier source in another language, so that the direction and approximate date of transfer can be stated. A dated Persian, Arabic or Latin witness of a saltpetre-based recipe earlier than the 1260s outside China would also count.
approach: Start from the recipe evidence historians have already gathered: the Chinese tradition from the Wujing zongyao onward in Needham (1986), the Latin Liber ignium as edited by Berthelot (1893) and dated by Partington (1960), the Arabic treatises of Ḥasan al-Rammāḥ discussed by al-Hassan (2003), and the fifteenth-century Feuerwerkbuch tradition now edited by Müller (2024). Note for each which manuscripts or printings the dating rests on.

Build a comparative corpus of every dated gunpowder and saltpetre recipe in Chinese, Arabic, Persian, Hebrew and Latin, transcribed from page images such as those in the Chinese Text Project and on Gallica, with specialists in each language checking agent transcriptions.

Normalise each recipe into structured data: ingredient proportions, technical vocabulary and purification method. Terms such as Arabic bārūd or Latin sal petrosum shifted in meaning, so each should carry its attested senses rather than a single modern equivalent.

Test the rival accounts against this corpus: direct transmission from China through the Mongols, as Needham (1986) and Andrade (2016) propose; an Arabic-Islamic intermediary stage, as al-Hassan (2003) argues; and the more cautious readings of Ayalon (1956), Hall (1997) and Haw (2013). Shared proportions, borrowed terms and common errors would indicate textual dependence; independent purification methods would weigh against it.

Even if the route stays uncertain, a dated, collated table of the earliest saltpetre purification methods and gunpowder ratios across traditions would sharpen the chronology. Because many witnesses are later copies, the dates of first appearance will often remain ranges.

Going further depends on libraries digitizing Arabic and Persian furūsiyya and military manuscripts in Paris, Istanbul, Cairo and elsewhere, and the earliest Latin Liber ignium and Feuerwerkbuch witnesses in the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek and the Royal Armouries, and on codicologists dating the copies.

title: How did Gutenberg cast his type?
short: Glyph-level variation in the earliest Mainz types has been read both as evidence against the punch, matrix and hand mould, and as fully compatible with it.
matters: The standard account of printing's origin credits Gutenberg with a system of steel punches, copper matrices and an adjustable hand mould, the method that let typefounders produce interchangeable sorts for the next four centuries. If the earliest Mainz types were instead cast from temporary or multiple matrices, the hand mould becomes a later development, possibly from the 1460s, and the chronology of technical invention, the roles of Gutenberg, Fust and Schoeffer, and comparisons with East Asian metal type all need revision. Methods for attributing and dating incunabula from type damage and sort identity also depend on what a 'single sort' is.
stuck: Agüera y Arcas and Needham's computational clustering of the DK type found far more distinct shapes per letter than a single-matrix system should produce, but their full data and methods were only partly published. Critics, above all Reske, argue that inking, paper, pressure, wear and photography generate apparent variation large enough to swamp the signal, so that algorithmic clustering of printed impressions cannot by itself identify matrices. No surviving type, punches or moulds from Gutenberg's shop exist, so the argument rests entirely on inferences from printed impressions.
solved: A published, reproducible dataset of every instance of selected letters across multiple copies of the DK-type prints and the 42-line Bible, with a casting model whose predicted distribution of within-letter variation matches the observed one significantly better than the alternatives, and which is consistent with impressions from experimentally cast type.
approach: The question has a long human history, from the punch-matrix-mould account of Carter (1969) and Needham (1982) to the DK-type clustering of Agüera y Arcas (2003), which suggested temporary matrices, and the microscopic rebuttal of Reske (2015). Computational work on the 42-line Bible by Alabert (2011), Rangel (2022) and Agata (2021) shows that glyph-level analysis is feasible, but each study used a small sample of letters and copies.

Segment and register every glyph instance from high-resolution digitizations of several B42 copies, including Göttingen and Keio, and of the surviving DK-type prints. The decision that shapes the data is how a glyph is aligned and measured, so the registration method and its error should be published before any clustering.

Separate variation that recurs at the same text position across copies, which points to inking, paper and press, from variation that recurs across positions, which points to the identity of a cast sort. A public catalogue of sorts that can be followed from page to page would be a lasting result even if the casting question stays open.

Simulate the competing processes: a single matrix with a hand mould, multiple matrices from one punch, temporary sand or clay matrices, and composite punches. Each predicts a different pattern of how many distinct shapes exist per letter and how they differ, and bibliographers and type historians should judge whether the fit is meaningful.

Decisive confirmation needs typefounders, printers and materials scientists willing to cast type by each candidate method, print with period materials, and pass the impressions through the same pipeline, alongside library partners prepared to image more copies at a common resolution.

title: How many people were carried in the Indian Ocean slave trades, 1500–1850?
short: European slave trading in the Indian Ocean has been tentatively counted, but the combined volume of Dutch, Portuguese, French, British, Arab, Swahili and South Asian trades remains unknown.
matters: Without a credible volume, the Indian Ocean cannot be compared with the Atlantic, and claims about the relative weight of African, Malagasy and Asian forced migration in global history rest on guesswork. The numbers bear on the labor regimes of the VOC settlements at Batavia and the Cape, the plantation economies of the Mascarenes, the clove economy of Zanzibar and Pemba, the Gulf pearl industry, and on the demographic history of Madagascar, Mozambique and the East African interior. They also bear on how abolition worked in practice, since the trade shifted to new routes and legal forms after British and French bans.
stuck: There is no voyage-level dataset for the Indian Ocean comparable to the SlaveVoyages trans-Atlantic database, and much of the traffic moved in small numbers aboard ships whose main cargo was something else, so it left little trace in shipping records. The evidence is spread across Dutch, Portuguese, French, English, Arabic, Persian, Gujarati and Swahili sources in archives on four continents, and many local trades (for example within the Indonesian archipelago or along the Swahili coast) were never systematically recorded. Existing estimates either cover only European traders, as in Richard Allen's tentative figure of roughly 570,000 to 730,000 people for 1500–1850, or rest on extrapolations from scattered nineteenth-century observations, as in Ralph Austen's census of the East African trade.
solved: An open, record-level database of documented slave voyages and transfers in the Indian Ocean for 1500–1850, with each record linked to its archival source, from which minimum counts by route, carrier and decade can be computed and gaps quantified, so that a total for all carriers can be stated with an explicit uncertainty range.
approach: Start from the carrier-by-carrier reconstructions historians have already built: Vink (2003) and Shell (1994) for the Dutch trade to Batavia and the Cape, Alpers (1975) and Machado (2014) for Mozambique and its Gujarati financiers, Sheriff (1987) and Vernet (2009) for the Swahili coast, Hopper (2015) for the Gulf, and Allen (2014) for all European carriers. Record the sources, method and coverage behind each figure, so that routes and decades with no count at all are explicit.

Define the unit of record before extracting anything. A voyage-level format suited to the Atlantic will miss most of this traffic, so the database should also hold small transfers, purchases and deeds aboard ships whose main cargo was something else, each linked to its archival source.

Pilot on the VOC Overgekomen Brieven en Papieren now searchable through GLOBALISE (2022), together with the Slave Office and transfer deeds in the Western Cape Archives. Agents can flag mentions of enslaved people and draft transfer records, with historians of the VOC reviewing them and checking totals against the estimates of Vink (2003) and Ward (2009). A documented minimum count for Dutch carriers by route and decade would be the first useful result.

Extend the method to the French Mascarene records, the T 71 slave registers for Mauritius and the Cape, and the FO 84 correspondence on the East African and Gulf trades, then test competing claims: that the Dutch trade was far larger than once assumed, as Vink (2003) argued, and that nineteenth-century exports from East Africa were of the order Austen (1988) inferred from scattered observations.

Model the all-carrier total as a range built route by route, with stated assumptions about the share of traffic that left no record, and publish the records and code so that specialists can revise any segment.

Progress beyond the Dutch and British material depends on new digitization with the Archives nationales d'outre-mer, the Arquivo Histórico Ultramarino, the National Archives of Mauritius and the Zanzibar National Archives, and on scholars who read Arabic, Gujarati, Persian and Swahili commercial papers.

title: Did anyone write down the Aceh tsunamis of c. 1394 and c. 1450?
short: Geology and archaeology show two great tsunamis struck northern Sumatra around 1394 and 1450, but no contemporary text describing either has been identified.
matters: Coral microatolls on Simeulue record sudden uplift above the Sunda megathrust in 1394 ± 2 and 1450 ± 3 CE, and tsunami deposits and abandoned settlements on the Aceh coast have been tied to these events, making them the closest predecessors of the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. A dated written witness would test the geological chronology independently, as Japanese records did for the 1700 Cascadia earthquake, and would constrain the extent of the events beyond Aceh (to Sri Lanka, South India or the Malay Peninsula), which matters for hazard models. It would also test the archaeological argument that the 1394 tsunami emptied the low-lying ports around Lamri and helped shift trade toward Samudera-Pasai and Melaka before the rise of the Aceh Sultanate.
stuck: The geological case was built after 2004 by earth scientists and archaeologists, and their historical discussion relies on indirect textual signals such as the fading of Lamri from Arabic sailing texts rather than on a search for a description of the event. The candidate sources are scattered across languages and genres: the Ming Shilu and Zheng He-era accounts (Ma Huan, Fei Xin, Gong Zhen), which describe Lamri and Samudera in the 1400s–1430s; Malay chronicles such as the Hikayat Raja Pasai and Sejarah Melayu, known only from much later copies and lacking dates; and Arabic, Persian and South Indian materials. Ming restrictions on private maritime trade from 1371 also thinned Chinese contact with Sumatra precisely around 1394, so silence in Chinese records is hard to interpret.
solved: Either a text written or reliably dated before c. 1520 that describes a sea flood, destructive wave or earthquake on the coasts of the eastern Indian Ocean and can be dated within the 1394 ± 2 or 1450 ± 3 CE windows; or a published negative search listing every source and passage examined for those windows (Ming Shilu, Zheng He-era accounts, Malay chronicles, Arabic nautical and geographical texts, Sri Lankan and South Indian records), with search terms and editions, so the absence can be cited and extended.
approach: Extract every Ming Shilu entry for 1385–1460 that names Lamri (Nanwuli, Nanboli), Samudera (Sumendala), Aru, Melaka or Ceylon from Geoff Wade's open-access translations (bulk use by arrangement with NUS Press) and the Chinese full text, and flag gaps in tribute missions, reports of envoys lost at sea, and any notices of floods or earthquakes reported by foreign missions.

Read Ma Huan's chapter on Nanboli (visited in the 1410s, where he reports only about a thousand households), together with Fei Xin and Gong Zhen, for signs of recent destruction, relocated settlement or altered coastline, and compare their descriptions with the pre-1394 sites mapped by Daly et al.

Search the Hikayat Raja Pasai, Sejarah Melayu and Acehnese chronicles in their manuscript witnesses for floods from the sea, abandoned towns or divine punishments by water, and test whether any episode can be anchored to the 1394 or 1450 windows by its reign context.
Query OpenITI and the Arabic nautical texts (Ibn Majid, Sulayman al-Mahri) for Lamri, Fansur and Mandara, and South Indian and Sri Lankan chronicles for coastal inundations in the same decades.

Pass every candidate passage, with its date range, to the Earth Observatory of Singapore team or other paleoseismologists, who can judge whether the described effects and location fit a Sunda megathrust source and the coral-dated windows.

title: How many Indigenous people were enslaved in the Americas between 1492 and 1900?
short: The best current estimate, 2.5 to 5 million enslaved Indigenous people, is the only hemispheric figure, and it rests on regional extrapolation rather than a count.
matters: The scale of Indigenous enslavement determines how far the demographic collapse of the Americas should be attributed to coerced labor, displacement and violence rather than to epidemic disease alone. It affects the comparison between Indigenous and African slavery in the colonial economies of the Caribbean, Brazil, Chile, northern Mexico, the American Southwest and the English colonies of the Southeast and New England. It also bears on how historians read Spanish and Portuguese abolitions of Indian slavery (1542, 1570, 1755) that were repeatedly evaded through categories such as just war, rescate, encomienda, peonage and 'adoption'.
stuck: Indigenous slavery was frequently illegal or ambiguously legal, so it was recorded under euphemisms (criados, piezas, naborías, administrados, captives) or not recorded at all, and it was dispersed across many small transactions rather than concentrated in shipping. The surviving evidence is scattered among notarial protocols, lawsuits, baptismal registers, probate inventories, military reports and Indigenous testimony in Spanish, Portuguese, French, English and Indigenous languages, mostly undigitized or uncatalogued at item level. Reséndez's 2.5–5 million figure, which he presents as a cautious range, therefore aggregates regional estimates of very different quality, and several regions (Amazonia, the Río de la Plata, Central America after 1550) have no systematic count.
solved: A published, source-linked database of individual enslaved Indigenous people and enslaving events, organized by region and period, from which documented minimums can be computed and combined with explicit, testable multipliers for under-recording, producing a hemispheric range that others can recompute region by region.
approach: Start from the regional reconstructions historians have already built, among them Jara (1971) on Mapuche captives in Chile, Monteiro (1988) on the Paulista captive economy, Gallay (2002) on the English Southeast, Trudel's (1990) name-by-name register of enslaved people in French Canada, roughly two-thirds of them Indigenous, and Stone (2021) on the early Spanish Caribbean. Record for each the sources, method and coverage behind the figures that Reséndez (2016) aggregates, so that the regions with no systematic count are explicit.

Build with regional specialists a glossary of the terms under which bondage was recorded (indio esclavo, pieza, naboría, criado, administrado, panis, gentio da terra), dated and placed, since many of these terms also described free or semi-free people and the same word could mean different statuses in different places.

Pilot on series that are partly digitized and already well studied, such as the Escribanos de Santiago and Real Audiencia records for the period of legal Mapuche slavery (1608–1683), on which Valenzuela Márquez (2017) and his collaborators have worked, or the Spanish Archives of New Mexico. Agents can transcribe, flag candidate entries and link the same person across sales, baptisms, lawsuits and inventories, with historians reviewing each link and checking totals against published regional counts.

Use the overlap between record types in these pilots to estimate how many enslaved people a given series misses. That correction is what turns a list of documented individuals into a population estimate.

Model the hemispheric total as a range built up region by region, each with stated assumptions about record survival and under-registration, and publish the linked records and code so that other teams can revise any region.

Extending this beyond the pilots depends on archives digitizing notarial and judicial series in Seville, Mexico City, Lima, São Paulo and Santa Fe, and on working with Indigenous communities, and with projects such as Native Bound Unbound that are already assembling records of enslaved people, on how those records are described and used.

title: Does the Indus script encode language, or a non-linguistic sign system?
short: Whether the short Harappan inscriptions record speech at all has been argued with entropy statistics for two decades; no test yet separates writing from emblem systems decisively.
matters: If the Indus signs are writing, the Harappan civilization was literate and every proposed decipherment (Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, Munda or other) is a legitimate project; if not, it becomes the main case of a large urban society administered without writing, which changes comparative accounts of states and bureaucracy. The answer also governs how seals, tags and pot inscriptions are read as evidence for trade, taxation and identity across a region of perhaps a million square kilometres.
stuck: Inscriptions average about five signs and the longest have only a few dozen, so statistical signatures that distinguish languages from other systems are weak at this length. Farmer, Sproat and Witzel (2004) argued the brevity and sign-repetition patterns are incompatible with writing; Rao et al. (2009) answered that conditional entropy places the corpus within the range of linguistic scripts; Sproat (2010, 2014) showed that several non-linguistic systems also fall in that range. The corpora used by different teams differ in sign lists (roughly 400 to 700 signs) and inclusion rules, and the most complete database (ICIT) requires permission to access.
solved: A pre-registered battery of measures, fixed before the Indus data are scored, classifies a large set of known writing systems and non-linguistic systems (heraldry, mason's marks, deity symbols, administrative codes) correctly when all are trimmed to the Indus length distribution, and then assigns the Indus corpus to one class with stated error rates that are robust to choice of sign list.
approach: The corpus rests on decades of human labour: the concordance of Mahadevan (1977), the photographic volumes of the CISI edited by Joshi (1987), Shah (1991) and Parpola (2010), and the ICIT database described by Wells (2015) and Fuls (2023). The statistical debate runs from Farmer (2004) through Rao (2009), Yadav (2010), Lee (2010) and Sproat (2010) to Sproat (2014) and Nair (2026).

Reconcile the Mahadevan, CISI and ICIT sign lists into an open, versioned corpus with a concordance between numbering systems. How variant signs are merged or split is the decision that shapes every later statistic, so alternatives should be kept side by side rather than settled silently.

Build comparison corpora of known scripts and non-linguistic systems, sampled to match Indus text lengths, object types and sign inventories, extending the dataset of Sproat (2014). Short texts are the core difficulty, since many measures that separate language from emblem systems lose power on inscriptions of five signs or fewer.

The linguistic and non-linguistic hypotheses should be tested on what they predict differently, such as sign-position regularities, reuse of sequences across object types and sites, and behaviour on longer texts, rather than on entropy alone.

Fix the classifiers and thresholds in a public pre-registration, then report results across alternative segmentations and sign lists. The outcome will likely be a graded likelihood rather than a verdict, and epigraphers and linguists should review it before it is cited.

Progress depends on negotiated open access to ICIT and to the CISI photographic archive, and on recording unpublished excavated material held by the Archaeological Survey of India and the Department of Archaeology and Museums, Pakistan.

title: How many people were killed in the Irish rising of 1641?
short: Contemporary claims of 154,000 to 300,000 Protestant victims are rejected, but the modern figure of roughly 4,000 killed has never been built from a full victim-level count.
matters: The scale of settler deaths in the winter of 1641–42 shaped English and Scottish policy toward Ireland for a decade, was invoked to justify the Cromwellian conquest and the land confiscations of the 1650s, and remained a fixed point in Protestant and Catholic memory into the twentieth century. Whether the violence amounted to a general massacre, a set of local atrocities, or something in between bears on arguments about colonial violence, sectarian identity, and the comparative history of early modern mass killing. A defensible total, with its distribution in time and place, would also show how far the printed atrocity literature departed from the sworn testimony on which it drew.
stuck: The figures in circulation were produced for polemic: the Lords Justices relayed a claim of 154,000 dead in 1643, Sir John Temple in 1646 wrote of over 300,000 British and Protestants murdered or expelled, and Sir William Petty later proposed about 37,000. Modern estimates, generally around 4,000 killed directly and perhaps 10,000–12,000 including deaths from exposure, hunger and disease, are largely concentrated on Ulster and rest on partial readings rather than a systematic count; Aidan Clarke argued in 2013 that even this consensus needs re-examination. The depositions are dominated by hearsay, the same killings are reported by many deponents with varying names and numbers, and Catholic victims of settler and army reprisals are poorly represented in a source collected from Protestants.
solved: A published, deduplicated database of every death reported in the 1641 Depositions, each linked to the depositions that mention it and coded for eyewitness versus hearsay, place, date and manner, yielding a reproducible minimum count and a stated range for Protestant deaths, with Catholic deaths assessed from other sources.
approach: Build on the transcription and imaging of the depositions at 1641.tcd.ie and the county-by-county Irish Manuscripts Commission edition, Clarke (2014), and on the arguments over their reliability in Perceval-Maxwell (1978), Clarke (2013), the essays in Darcy (2012) and Gibney (2013). The Down Survey project, Ó Siochrú (2013), has already mapped many reported murders and assaults, and the Aberdeen corpus work of MacLeod (2012) shows how the testimony can be read linguistically.

Turn each deposition into structured records of reported killings: victims, perpetrators, place, date and, above all, whether the deponent was an eyewitness or repeating hearsay. That grading matters most, since much of the inflation in Temple (1646) and later counts rests on second-hand reports.

Normalise personal and place names against seventeenth-century gazetteers and the Down Survey parish and barony maps, then cluster reports of the same event across depositions so that one killing told by five refugees is counted once.

Before attempting any national figure, build a deduplicated, graded register for a single well-documented county such as Armagh, from TCD MS 836, and test it against the 1650s High Court of Justice examinations taken for prosecutions. That alone would show how far eyewitness and hearsay totals diverge.

Weigh the rival estimates, from the tens or hundreds of thousands claimed in print by Temple (1646) and Hickson (1884) to the low thousands proposed by modern historians, against the register. Add reprisal killings of Catholics from army reports in the State Papers, the Ormond correspondence and the pamphlet literature, so the total is two-sided; it will remain a range bounded by how hearsay is treated.

Historians of early modern Ireland should set the matching and weighting rules and review uncertain clusters and every agent-produced record. The work depends on Trinity College Dublin keeping the 1641 data open and on access to the Bodleian and Kew papers, which are not yet fully digitized.

title: How many people did the Justinianic Plague kill, and did it change late antique society?
short: Ancient DNA confirms Yersinia pestis caused the First Pandemic (541–c.750), but estimates of its mortality and long-term consequences range from catastrophic to modest.
matters: Maximalist readings make the pandemic a cause of the end of antiquity: depopulation weakening the eastern Roman empire before the Arab conquests, contraction of cities and trade, and the rural and fiscal transformations of the seventh century. Minimalist readings remove that causal link and return explanatory weight to war, climate and political decisions. The answer also shapes comparisons with the Black Death and with modern pandemics, and the use of plague as a general explanation in historical narratives.
stuck: Narrative sources (Procopius, John of Ephesus, Evagrius, Gregory of Tours) give vivid but rhetorically shaped figures for a few cities, and there are almost no serial demographic records. Documentary proxies such as papyri, legislation, coin output, inscriptions and building activity can be read as showing disruption or continuity depending on the baseline chosen. Ancient DNA proves presence of the pathogen at particular sites but not mortality rates, and pollen and settlement data are often too coarse in date to isolate the 540s from other causes.
solved: A region-by-region database of dated proxies (papyri, legislation, coin issues, dated inscriptions, burials with plague DNA, high-resolution pollen cores, settlement and building chronologies) showing, with stated uncertainties, whether measurable discontinuities cluster at the documented plague waves more than expected from a baseline of other shocks, yielding bounded mortality estimates for named regions.
approach: Build on the source surveys of Biraben (1969) and Stathakopoulos (2004), the essays in Little (2007), and the maximalist synthesis of Harper (2017), read against the minimalist critique of Mordechai and Eisenberg (2019) and the replies by Sarris (2021) and Meier (2020). Roosen (2018) is a warning about reusing older compilations of plague mentions without returning to the sources.

Extract and date every reference to plague waves in narrative and documentary sources, then count dated papyri from the Papyrological Navigator, inscriptions, laws and coin issues per year and region. The main decision is how to separate a genuine fall in documentation from the uneven survival of sources, so every series needs an explicit pre-541 baseline.

Two readings compete: a demographic catastrophe that reshaped the empire, and a serious but locally bounded epidemic. Event-study comparisons around each wave would tell them apart: a maximalist case predicts synchronous breaks across regions and source types, a minimalist one scattered or absent breaks.

Align these series with pathogen genomes from Harbeck (2013), Wagner (2014) and Keller (2019), with pollen records in Neotoma, and with site studies such as Bar-Oz (2019) and Hendrix (2026). Epidemic models like White (2020), which found the reported Constantinople mortality and duration hard to reconcile, can test whether source claims are internally plausible.

A dated, region-by-region register of attested outbreaks and documentary series would be useful even if mortality stays unresolved. Any death toll will remain a wide range that differs by region rather than a single imperial figure.

Late antique historians, papyrologists and numismatists should review the coding and any agent-produced counts. Confirmation depends on ancient-DNA laboratories screening more burials across the Mediterranean and Near East, and on palynologists producing well-dated, high-resolution cores.

title: Did Kerala-school infinite series reach early modern Europe through Jesuit missionaries?
short: Madhava's school derived power series for π, sine and cosine before 1500; whether Jesuits in Kerala carried them to Europe remains undocumented.
matters: If Kerala results on infinite series reached Europe, accounts of the origins of the calculus in Gregory, Newton and Leibniz would need to include an Indian component rather than parallel discovery. The question has also become a test case for arguments about the standard of evidence applied to East-to-West versus West-to-East transmission, and for the role of Jesuit colleges as intermediaries in Asian knowledge more generally.
stuck: The Kerala results (attributed to Mādhava, c. 1340–1425, and preserved in Nīlakaṇṭha's Tantrasaṅgraha of 1501 and Jyeṣṭhadeva's Yuktibhāṣā of c. 1530) are securely dated, and Jesuits were present in Cochin from the mid-sixteenth century. But no Jesuit letter, translation, notebook or library record yet produced mentions these series, and Joseph himself reports that a survey of Jesuit literature found no direct trace. The Jesuit college library at Cochin was dispersed when the Dutch took the city in 1663, and relevant Malayalam and Sanskrit manuscripts are scattered and only partly catalogued.
solved: Either a dated document showing a European in possession of, or describing, a Kerala series result before Gregory (1668) and Newton (c. 1665–1669), or a documented, bounded search of the named Jesuit correspondence series (ARSI Goa and Malabar volumes, Documenta Indica, Clavius correspondence) and Kerala manuscript holdings that records the absence of any such reference.
approach: Build on the mathematical reconstructions of the Kerala school from Whish (1834) and Rajagopal (1978) to the edition and translation of the Yuktibhāṣā in Sarma (2008) and the surveys of Plofker (2009) and Divakaran (2018). The transmission case is argued most fully in Joseph (2009) and Raju (2007), and questioned in Bressoud (2002) and Plofker (2009).

Read the printed Documenta Indica and the microfilmed ARSI Goa-Malabar letters, located through Gramatowski (1992), for references to Indian astronomy, calendars, Brahmin informants and mathematical manuscripts. Županov (2005) and Baldini (2008) give the missionary and scientific context for which Jesuits were in Cochin and what they were trained to notice.

Turn these into a register of named Jesuits, places, dates and the subject of each mention, then cross-match it against the Clavius correspondence edited by Baldini (1992) and other Collegio Romano correspondents. Deciding what counts as a mathematical reference, as opposed to calendrical or astrological interest, shapes the result and should be set by specialists.

In parallel, survey Kerala astronomical manuscripts at the Oriental Research Institute and the Royal Asiatic Society for ownership marks, copying notes or Latin and Portuguese annotations that would show European hands.

The hypotheses are direct transmission through Jesuit intermediaries, independent European rediscovery, and diffuse exposure too thin to trace. Only a named intermediary, a manuscript copy in Europe or a European text echoing Kerala methods would decide between them, so a well-documented absence in the Jesuit record would itself be a result.

Historians of Indian mathematics and Jesuit specialists should review every match. Progress depends on item-level digitization of the ARSI Goa series and on the Oriental Research Institute and Royal Asiatic Society completing searchable catalogues of their palm-leaf holdings.

title: Do khipus record more than numbers, and can their non-numerical signs be read?
short: Andean knotted cords encode numbers in a known decimal system; whether colour, ply, attachment and knot direction also record names, categories or narrative remains open.
matters: Colonial chroniclers reported that khipukamayuq read histories, genealogies and laws from cords. If khipus encoded non-numerical information systematically, the Inka state kept records that could be read as primary sources for Andean history before and after 1532, and the comparative history of writing would need to include a non-graphic system. If they did not, accounts of Inka administration must explain how a large empire functioned on numerical records plus memory.
stuck: Roughly a thousand khipus survive (estimates vary), most without archaeological context, and very few can be paired with a Spanish-language transcription of the same record. The decimal knot system was established by Locke (1912) and the Aschers, but colour, fibre, spin and ply, attachment direction and knot orientation vary in ways that have resisted consistent interpretation. Data were long scattered across incompatible recording schemes and unpublished notebooks.
solved: A model trained on matched khipu–document pairs predicts, for khipus or transcriptions held out from training, non-numerical features (such as moiety, lineage, place or personal-name categories) significantly better than chance and better than numerical-only baselines, and the predictions are confirmed when new matched pairs are found.
approach: Build on the structural studies of Locke (1912), Ascher (2005) and Urton (2005), the ethnography of Salomon (2004), and the colonial transcriptions gathered in Pärssinen (2004). Recent work has opened the non-numerical question directly: Hyland (2017) on Collata, Clindaniel (2019) on paired signs at Inkawasi, and Medrano (2018) on the Santa Valley khipus.

Use the Open Khipu Repository and the Khipu Field Guide as a common schema. Medrano (2024) shows how far the arithmetic regularities of the corpus can be characterised at scale, which sets a baseline any non-numerical reading must go beyond.

Search colonial visitas, revisitas and court records in Peruvian and Spanish archives, including the Archivo General de la Nación, for documents stating that their figures were read from khipus. Each candidate pair, matched by totals and structure, is a small key; a vetted list of such pairs would be useful whatever it yields for decipherment.

Test rival readings against held-out cord groups, for example the alternative moiety and hierarchy alignments of Medrano (2018) and FitzPatrick (2024). The deciding evidence is whether a proposed meaning for colour, ply or attachment predicts unseen cords better than chance.
Expect a mixed answer: some signs may prove to be category or name markers, while narrative khipus such as those at Collata stay only partly read.

Andeanists, khipu specialists and the communities that hold khipus should review every proposed reading. The work depends on recording undocumented khipus in museum stores, especially in Berlin, Lima and smaller Peruvian collections, and on agreements with communities such as Collata and Rapaz.

title: What language does Linear A record, and can any proposed family beat chance?
short: Minoan Linear A can be roughly sounded out through Linear B values, but no proposed language family has been shown to fit better than random controls.
matters: The language of Linear A bears on who the Minoans were, how Bronze Age Crete related to Anatolia, the Levant and Egypt, and what the Mycenaean Greeks inherited when they adapted the script as Linear B. Readings of personal names, toponyms and religious formulae on libation vessels would change accounts of Minoan religion and administration. A demonstration that no candidate family is detectable at this corpus size would also be a result, setting limits on what further comparative claims can mean.
stuck: The corpus is small and mostly administrative: about 1,430 documents in the original GORILA edition and 1,534 after the 2024–25 supplement, most of them short tallies, sealings and roundels, with roughly 7,500 signs in all. Linear B values give approximate pronunciations, but the transfer of values is itself an assumption, and many proposals (Luwian, Semitic, Hurrian, Tyrsenian and others) have been argued by selective lexical matching without controls for how many matches chance would produce. Few proposals have been stated in advance in a form that could fail.
solved: A language-family hypothesis, specified before testing (sound correspondences, morphology, lexicon), predicts readings of held-out inscriptions significantly better than the same procedure applied to shuffled sign values and unrelated control languages; or a power analysis shows that no such test can succeed at the current corpus size. A narrower solvable target is a complete, consistent account of the fraction signs and commodity totals (KU-RO) that balances the surviving tallies.
approach: The corpus is already well curated: Godart and Olivier (1976) and the supplement of Del Freo and Zurbach (2025) fix the texts, Salgarella and Castellan (2020) and lineara.xyz make them searchable, and Davis (2014) has edited the inscribed stone vessels that carry the libation formula. A first task is a single concordance across these, with transliteration uncertainty recorded sign by sign rather than resolved silently.

Which Linear B sound values to carry over is the decision that shapes every later test. Following Salgarella (2020), the corpus can be encoded in tiers, from values that are palaeographically secure to those that are merely assumed, so that each hypothesis is scored on the tier it depends on.

The accounting layer can be solved independently of the language. Extending Bennett (1950) and Corazza et al. (2021), fraction values and logogram totals can be treated as constraints that every complete tally ending in ku-ro must satisfy, as on HT 13, HT 85a and HT 94a; a balanced set of values would be useful even if no word is ever read.

The rival family hypotheses, Anatolian after Palmer (1958) and Finkelberg (1990), Semitic after Gordon (1966), and a non-Indo-European isolate favoured by Davis (2026), can each be written as an explicit generative model and pre-registered before scoring.

Each model is then scored against held-out texts using the cognate-alignment methods of Luo et al. (2019) and Luo et al. (2021), with the fictitious value assignments of Packard (1974) as a chance baseline. Scattered matches of the kind reported by Nepal and Perono Cacciafoco (2024) count only if they beat that baseline; the likeliest honest outcome is that every family is ranked, with intervals, rather than one confirmed.

Aegean epigraphers should review both the encoding and the scoring, ideally through the INSCRIBE project at Bologna, and permits to recheck doubtful signs on originals in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum would tighten the uncertain tier.

title: How many early printed editions have been lost without trace?
short: Estimates of the share of fifteenth- and sixteenth-century editions that survive in no copy vary widely, and depend on statistical models that have rarely been tested against later discoveries.
matters: Quantitative histories of the early book trade, of literacy and of the spread of ideas count surviving editions as if they were a fixed fraction of what was printed. If loss was heavy and uneven, falling hardest on cheap, small-format, vernacular, ephemeral and heavily used books such as schoolbooks, almanacs, broadsides and devotional texts, then the apparent dominance of Latin learned printing and the relative output of regions and printers are artefacts of survival. The same estimates are used to calibrate long-run series of book production that feed into economic history.
stuck: Lost editions leave evidence only indirectly, in booksellers' catalogues, inventories, references, binding fragments and editions known from a single copy. Statistical estimates depend on assumptions about how copy counts are distributed, and the main models give different answers for different categories of book. Catalogues such as ISTC, GW and USTC are revised continuously, but no one has systematically used their revision history to test whether past estimates correctly predicted the rate and kind of new discoveries.
solved: A survival model fitted on a dated snapshot of a major catalogue (for example ISTC or USTC as of a past year) that correctly predicts the number and category distribution of editions added in later years, together with an estimate of total lost editions by format, language and genre with stated uncertainty.
approach: The estimates so far rest on a few decisions made differently each time: Buringh and van Zanden (2009) applied assumed loss rates, Green et al. (2011) and Green and McIntyre (2016) fitted copy-count distributions from ISTC, and Kestemont and Karsdorp (2020) and Kestemont et al. (2022) brought ecological unseen-species estimators from Efron and Thisted (1976) to manuscripts, with open code. Camps, Randon-Furling and Godreau (2025) have since set manuscript and incunable loss rates side by side.

Turning the catalogues into data means one record per edition with its surviving copy count, format, language, genre and sheet count. How copies are counted shapes the result, since fragments in bindings, Sammelbände and duplicate holdings in aggregated catalogues all inflate or deflate the singletons on which the estimators depend; Proot (2016) shows why sheet count and institutional ownership belong in the model.

With that table built from ISTC, GW, USTC and VD16, Chao1, Efron–Thisted and their successors can be fitted separately by format, language and genre, so that cheap vernacular print, which Pettegree (2016) and Eisermann (2016) argue is the most heavily lost, is not averaged away.

Catalogues have histories, so the estimators can be tested. Reconstructing earlier states of ISTC and GW from published versions and dated records, and checking what each snapshot predicted against the editions found since, would show which estimator is calibrated; that comparison is useful whatever the final total.

The documentary record of lost books is a second, independent check: registered titles in the Stationers' Register as used by Hill (2016), booksellers' lists, inventories and privileges, as gathered by Bruni and Pettegree (2016). Where statistical and documentary estimates diverge, the gap itself measures how far copy-count models miss editions that left no survivor at all, and the total will remain a range.

The catalogues are online, so no new digitization is needed, but dated record histories depend on cooperation from their maintainers at CERL, the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin and St Andrews, and book historians should review how fragments and ephemera are classified.
