title: Were Mendel's pea-hybrid data too close to expectation, and if so, why?
short: Fisher showed in 1936 that Mendel's ratios fit theory improbably well; a century of explanations has not produced documentary evidence of how the counts were made.
matters: Mendel's paper is the founding document of genetics and a standard case in teaching about scientific integrity, so whether his numbers were selected, adjusted, unconsciously biased or simply lucky affects how the episode is taught and how historians read his intentions. The answer also bears on what Mendel set out to do, whether he tested a pre-formed theory or reported plant-breeding experiments, and on the reception of his work by Nägeli and the rediscoverers of 1900.
stuck: Fisher's chi-square analysis found an overall fit with a probability of roughly 7 in 100,000 and also argued that Mendel's 2:1 ratios in the progeny tests should have been biased toward 1.7:1. Mendel's experimental notebooks do not survive, and many of his papers are reported to have been burned after his death in 1884, so only the published paper and a handful of letters to Nägeli constrain explanations. Proposed solutions (a too-eager assistant, sequential stopping, selective reporting, a different sampling model, botanical factors such as pollen tetrads) are each compatible with the summary numbers and therefore hard to discriminate.
solved: Either discovery of primary records (field notes, seed counts, or correspondence) that show how Mendel collected and selected his counts, or a statistical analysis that specifies a historically documented procedure and shows that it reproduces both Fisher's goodness-of-fit anomaly and the 2:1 progeny-test anomaly at conventional significance, while competing procedures do not.
approach: Begin from the statistical literature that already exists: Weldon (1902) and Fisher (1936) on the excess of good fits, Edwards (1986) on the distribution of chi-square values, Novitski (2004) on the 2:1 progeny tests, Pires and Branco (2010) on repeated experiments, and the reassessment of the segregation ratios by Ellis et al. (2019). The collected papers in Franklin et al. (2008) give a common starting point.

Encode every count in the 1866 paper and the letters to Nägeli as a single dataset, checking the German text and page images on MendelWeb against the manuscript held by the Mendel Museum. Much depends on how one divides the reported totals into experimental units, since the chi-square results depend on whether counts are treated per plant, per experiment or pooled.

Reproduce the published models in one shared framework and state which assumptions each depends on. That alone would be a useful intermediate result: a public, rerunnable comparison of the main explanations on identical data.

Test the rival hypotheses against both anomalies at once: an assistant who knew the expected ratios, sequential stopping or repetition of deviant experiments, selective reporting, a different sampling model for the progeny tests, and botanical effects such as tetrad pollen, which Fairbanks and Schaalje (2007) tested experimentally and did not find. Without new documents the answer is likely to remain a set of procedures compatible with the data rather than a single verdict, and Radick (2022) is a reminder that the framing of the question has its own history.

Search the records of the abbey, the Brno natural-history society, local schools and horticultural societies for mentions of assistants, seed exchanges and garden practice, and the papers of Nägeli and other correspondents for unpublished material, with Czech and German specialists reviewing any candidate finds.

Progress on the documentary side depends on the Mendelianum, the Augustinian Abbey and Czech and German archives making their holdings searchable and digitized, and on plant geneticists willing to run growing and counting trials that test the botanical explanations directly.

title: Can the Meroitic language be translated beyond its funerary formulae?
short: Meroitic script has been readable since Griffith's work of 1909–1911, but outside formulaic texts the language of the Kingdom of Kush is still largely untranslated.
matters: Meroitic is the oldest written language of sub-Saharan Africa and the administrative and royal language of Kush for some seven centuries. The long royal stelae, temple texts and chronicles almost certainly record wars with Rome, succession and religious practice from a Kushite point of view; at present historians rely on Greek, Latin and Egyptian sources for that history. A secure classification would also date the spread of Northern East Sudanic languages along the Nile, which bears on Nubian linguistic and population history.
stuck: The script's sound values were recovered from Egyptian names, but there is no substantial bilingual text, and the language has no close, well-documented descendant. Most of the corpus consists of funerary inscriptions with predictable formulae, so the vocabulary securely understood is small, by most accounts on the order of a hundred words, and grammar is reconstructed mainly from those formulae. Classification is disputed: Rilly argues for the Northern East Sudanic branch with Nubian, Nara, Taman and Nyima, while Rowan and Lipiński have argued for an Afroasiatic affiliation.
solved: A lexicon and grammar, fixed before testing, yield translations of held-out non-funerary passages (for example sections of royal stelae or temple texts) that independent specialists judge consistent with their archaeological, iconographic and historical context, and that correctly predict content later confirmed by newly found or newly published inscriptions.
approach: Since Griffith (1911) read the script, progress has come from the formulae and from comparison. The REM corpus of Leclant et al. (2000), Rilly (2007) on the lexicon and grammar, Rilly (2010) on the language family, and Rilly (2012), written with Alex de Voogt, are the base, with Rilly (2020) showing how verbal morphology can be recovered through Nubian.

The REM texts and inscriptions published since 2000 need to become a lemmatized, machine-readable corpus with find context, object type and date. Segmentation is the decision that matters most, since the word divider is used inconsistently, and every split the corpus adopts should be traceable to an editor.

Two classifications compete: the Northern East Sudanic affiliation argued in Rilly (2010), and the Afroasiatic reading of the phonology in Rowan (2015). Each predicts different cognates for the basic vocabulary, and Blench (2020) bears on how secure the East Sudanic family itself is, so the corpus can score both against the same held-out vocabulary.

Reconstructed Proto-Northern East Sudanic and the Old Nubian lexicon of Browne (1996) can then generate constrained translation hypotheses, tested on passages whose context predicts part of the content: offering scenes, lists of places, and military iconography as on the Hamadab stela of Amanirenas and Akinidad.

A useful intermediate result is a graded glossary that separates secure, probable and conjectural meanings for every recurring word outside the funerary formulae. Royal and historical texts will likely stay partly readable, with the meaning of many passages given as a range of candidates rather than a single translation.

This depends on Nubian and Nilo-Saharan linguists reviewing every proposal, and on excavation missions and museums sharing post-2000 inscriptions and photographs, a need sharpened by reported damage to collections in Khartoum during the war that began in 2023.

title: What is the absolute chronology of early second-millennium BCE Mesopotamia?
short: Competing High, Middle, Low and Ultra-Low chronologies place Hammurabi and the fall of Babylon up to about 150 years apart; no single model integrates all the evidence.
matters: The relative sequence of Old Assyrian, Old Babylonian and Kassite rulers is well established, but its anchor in absolute years is not, so every date before about 1400 BCE in Mesopotamia, Anatolia, Syria and the Levant inherits the uncertainty. Synchronisms with Egypt, the Hittite sack of Babylon, the dating of the Santorini eruption debate, climate-and-collapse arguments and comparisons with radiocarbon-dated archaeology all depend on which option is chosen. The four usual options put the fall of Babylon at 1651, 1595, 1531 or 1499 BCE.
stuck: The Venus observations preserved in later copies of Enūma Anu Enlil tablet 63 are corrupt and allow several solutions roughly 56 or 64 years apart, and month-length and eclipse arguments depend on contested readings and observational assumptions. Assyrian King List distance figures contain uncertain reign lengths, and the Kültepe eponym lists must be joined to Old Babylonian sources through a small number of synchronisms. Dendrochronological sequences from Anatolian sites were long only floating, and their wiggle-matched radiocarbon dates carry their own calibration and regional-offset uncertainties.
solved: A published, reproducible Bayesian model that ingests the Venus data, lunar month lengths, eclipse candidates, king-list and eponym-list distance numbers, dendrochronological sequences and radiocarbon dates with explicit priors, returns a posterior for a fixed anchor (such as Ammisaduqa year 1) with a stated uncertainty under 10 years, and remains stable when individual lines of evidence are removed.
approach: The textual framework is already well mapped: Pruzsinszky (2009) sets out the king lists, eponym lists, year names and synchronisms, Barjamovic, Hertel and Larsen (2012) rebuilt the Old Assyrian eponym sequence with the help of KEL G from Günbattı (2008), and Mebert (2010) re-edited every copy of the Venus observations preserved in later copies of Enūma Anu Enlil tablet 63. Teams can build directly on these, and on the dated texts in ARCHIBAB and the Old Assyrian Research Environment.

Compile one machine-readable dataset of every chronologically relevant datum: each Venus copy and its variant readings, month-length records from Old Babylonian archives, eponym-list entries, reign lengths and cross-dated synchronisms, each with full citation and a note on how secure the reading is. Deciding how to score a damaged or disputed reading will shape the result more than any later statistics.

The rival solutions, the High chronology of Langdon and Fotheringham (1928) and Huber (1982), the Middle and Low-Middle options argued by Barjamovic, Hertel and Larsen (2012) and de Jong (2013), and the Ultra-Low chronology of Gasche et al. (1998), each make predictions about Venus visibility, lunar month lengths and the spacing of Assyrian eponyms. Testing all of them against the same dataset, as Huber (2000) and Gurzadyan (2000) did against parts of it, would show where they genuinely diverge.

Encode the textual constraints alongside the dendro-radiocarbon wiggle-matches of Manning et al. (2016) in a Bayesian framework such as OxCal, described by Bronk Ramsey (2009), calibrated with IntCal20 from Reimer et al. (2020). Modelling the regional offsets identified by Manning et al. (2020) explicitly matters, since a few decades of offset is the size of the gap between neighbouring chronologies.

Sensitivity analysis is a useful result in its own right: it would show which tablets, readings and samples actually drive the answer, and which long-debated items make no difference. The answer will most likely remain a narrowed range of candidate dates rather than a single year, and Assyriologists and radiocarbon specialists should review both the coding and the model.

Settling the remaining range requires new radiocarbon and dendrochronological measurements on securely contexted short-lived samples and timbers from Kültepe, Acemhöyük and Babylonian sites, which depends on excavation teams, the Cornell Tree-Ring Laboratory and radiocarbon laboratories, and on museums allowing collation of the tablets themselves.

title: Did the population of Ottoman Anatolia collapse in the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries?
short: Tax surveys show rapid growth in Anatolia to about 1580, but whether the decline that followed was a demographic collapse or an artefact of changing registration remains unsettled.
matters: A large fall in Anatolian population would connect the Celali rebellions, the Little Ice Age droughts of the 1590s, rural flight and the transformation of Ottoman fiscal and military institutions into one crisis comparable to the 'general crisis' of seventeenth-century Europe and China. If the decline was smaller or mainly a shift from registered villages to towns, nomadism and untaxed settlements, then narratives of Ottoman 'decline' and of climate-driven collapse need revision. The question also tests whether Ottoman tax registers can be used for demography at all.
stuck: The detailed provincial surveys (tahrir defterleri) end in most of Anatolia by the 1580s and record taxable household heads rather than people, while the seventeenth-century avarız and cizye registers that follow count fiscal units (avarızhane) whose relation to households changed over time. Comparisons across the two series therefore mix demographic change with changes in what was counted. Most studies cover single districts, the registers are held in two archives with different access regimes, and many have never been transcribed.
solved: A linked village-level dataset across all surviving tahrir and avarız registers for a large sample of Anatolian districts, with a validated model converting each register's fiscal units into households, that produces regional population series from 1520 to 1700 with uncertainty and that agrees with independent evidence such as court records, settlement abandonment and cizye counts.
approach: The debate is already framed by decades of register work. Barkan (1957) and Cook (1972) read the sixteenth-century tahrirs as evidence of strong growth and pressure on land, Erder and Faroqhi (1979) located a turning point around the 1580s, and Özel (2004) and Özel (2016) linked late tahrirs to seventeenth-century avarız registers to argue for a deep, lasting decline. White (2011) tied that decline to drought, famine and the Celali rebellions described by Akdağ (1963) and Griswold (1983).

Much of the evidence is already transcribed in published district editions, such as the Kayseri registers edited by İnbaşı (2009), and in monographs issued by the Türk Tarih Kurumu. Collaborative teams could structure these into a common table of villages, household heads, bachelors and exempt groups, with every figure traced to a page of a register.

The core difficulty is that tahrir and avarız registers count different things, as Murphey (1990), Ataman (1992), Lowry (1992) and Coşgel (2004) emphasise. Where registers for the same district overlap, conversion factors between fiscal units and households can be estimated, and these should be carried forward as ranges rather than single multipliers.

Linking villages across registers and to modern locations would show where settlements were abandoned rather than merely re-registered. The nineteenth-century gazetteer of Kabadayı et al. (2022) offers a bridge between Ottoman toponyms and coordinates, and a mapped series for a few well-documented districts would be useful even if an empire-wide figure stays out of reach.

Two explanations then compete: real demographic collapse through violence, famine and flight, or an artefact of changing fiscal practice, with households hidden, merged into larger avarız units or moved outside the surveyed villages. Regional series can be tested against climate reconstructions, the timing of Celali violence and court-record evidence of flight and abandoned villages in İSAM's copies of the kadı registers, which would tend to confirm collapse where all three move together.

Scaling beyond published registers requires systematic digitization of the Tapu Tahrir (TT.d) and avarız series in the Ottoman Archives and the Kuyûd-ı Kadîme registers in Ankara, with archivists and Ottoman palaeographers. Many registers use siyakat numerals and chancery hands that need specialist verification, and automated transcription has so far been tested mainly on print, as in Kirmizialtin and Wrisley (2022).

title: Why did plague disappear from western Europe after the early eighteenth century?
short: After nearly four centuries of recurring epidemics, plague retreated from western and central Europe between the 1660s and the 1720s while persisting in the Ottoman Mediterranean, and no explanation commands agreement.
matters: The retreat of plague is one of the earliest large declines in European mortality, and its cause determines whether early modern states could control epidemic disease through quarantine, cordons and health passes, or whether the decline was ecological or biological and owed little to policy. The answer bears on demographic models of the eighteenth-century population rise, on the divergence between western Europe and the Ottoman and Russian lands where plague continued into the nineteenth century, and on current arguments about the efficacy of border controls against epidemics.
stuck: The retreat was gradual and uneven: London's last major epidemic was 1665, central Europe and the Baltic suffered in 1708–13, Provence in 1720–22, Messina in 1743, Moscow in 1771, and Noja (1815–16) and Mallorca (1820) saw late seaborne outbreaks, so any explanation must account for a moving frontier rather than a single date. Each main hypothesis (quarantine, rat or flea ecology, host immunity, climate, pathogen change) predicts the same broad outcome and is hard to falsify from mortality data alone. The genetic evidence has opened a parallel dispute over whether European plague was sustained by local reservoirs or repeatedly reintroduced from Asia, and ancient DNA samples remain few for the last outbreaks.
solved: A spatially explicit model, fitted to dated outbreak records and to the records of health offices on ship arrivals, quarantines and cordons, that reproduces the sequence and geography of the last western European outbreaks and correctly predicts which ports and regions escaped introduction when exposed, with its assumptions about reservoirs consistent with the ancient DNA phylogeny.
approach: Build a georeferenced, dated catalogue of plague outbreaks from 1650 to 1850 across Europe and the Mediterranean, starting from Biraben's inventory and extending it with regional studies, bills of mortality and parish registers, with source citations for every entry.

Extract arrivals, origins, bills of health, quarantine durations and lazaretto incidents from the health office archives of Marseille, Venice, Livorno, Genoa, Dubrovnik and Malta, which together record many near-misses where infected ships were stopped; much of this requires new digitization, building on the online Marseille captains' declarations of 1709–1852.

Link these to Levant shipping and consular reports of plague in Ottoman ports to estimate exposure for each European port by year, and test whether quarantine stringency, rather than exposure, explains which ports escaped.

Work with palaeogeneticists to sample burials from the last outbreaks (Provence, the Baltic, Messina, southern Italy, the Balkans) and with ecologists on rodent and flea faunal remains, so that reservoir and reintroduction scenarios can be tested against the documentary model.

title: Does Proto-Elamite record language, and is it the ancestor of Linear Elamite?
short: Iran's earliest script survives on about 1,600–1,700 accounting tablets; its numbers are read, but whether its other signs write words, and how it relates to Linear Elamite, is disputed.
matters: Proto-Elamite is one of the earliest scripts anywhere and the first on the Iranian plateau, so its nature bears on whether writing was invented once in Mesopotamia and borrowed, or developed independently in more than one place. If its non-numerical signs encode syllables of Elamite, the history of that language extends back almost a millennium. Desset and colleagues' 2022 decipherment of Linear Elamite rests partly on a claimed continuity from Proto-Elamite; whether that continuity holds affects how far the decipherment can be pushed back.
stuck: The tablets are almost all administrative accounts from Susa, with smaller groups from Tepe Yahya, Tal-i Malyan, Tepe Sofalin and other sites; they contain several hundred non-numerical signs and short entries dominated by numbers. The numerical systems were largely worked out by Damerow and Englund through comparison with Mesopotamian proto-cuneiform, but the remaining signs could be logograms, personal names, institutional labels or syllables, and the short entries offer few repeated phonetic contexts. More than five centuries separate the last Proto-Elamite tablets from the first Linear Elamite inscriptions, and Dahl (2023) argues that Linear Elamite was a deliberate new creation rather than a descendant.
solved: A structural analysis that partitions the sign inventory into numerical, logographic and candidate phonetic signs, with stated criteria, is validated on proto-cuneiform where the answers are known; applied to Proto-Elamite, it either identifies a set of signs whose distribution fits a syllabary, with predicted values that cohere with Linear Elamite readings beyond chance, or shows that no such subset exists.
approach: Start from the CDLI transliterations and images, and treat the numerical layer as a solved constraint system so that every tablet's arithmetic is checked and the residual signs isolated.

Train sign-distribution models on proto-cuneiform and early cuneiform, where logograms, determinatives and phonetic complements are known, then test whether Proto-Elamite contains a comparable phonetic subset, following the computational work of Born, Kelley and colleagues.
Test the claimed Linear Elamite relation with pre-registered sign-form and value correspondences against shuffled pairings.
Unpublished and poorly imaged tablets in the Louvre and in Iranian collections need high-resolution imaging, which requires collaboration with those institutions.

title: Did Ptolemy observe the Almagest star catalogue or adapt Hipparchus's?
short: Ptolemy's catalogue of about 1,025 stars claims his own observations; statistical anomalies suggest much of it derives from Hipparchus three centuries earlier.
matters: The Almagest catalogue is the oldest fully preserved star catalogue and the basis of Western and Islamic stellar astronomy until Ulugh Beg. Whether it records new observations bears on Ptolemy's reliability as a witness to his own practice, on the reconstruction of Hipparchus's lost catalogue, on the value of ancient positions for measuring precession and proper motion, and on broader arguments about how ancient scientists used data.
stuck: Ptolemy dates the catalogue to the first year of Antoninus (AD 137) and implies he observed it, but its longitudes are systematically about 1° too small for that date, consistent with adding a precession of 1° per century to positions for Hipparchus's epoch. Statistical tests of epoch, observer latitude, rounding patterns and error structure have yielded conflicting verdicts because the catalogue may mix sources and because results depend on modelling choices. Until 2022 there were almost no direct Hipparchan coordinates against which to compare.
solved: Recovery of enough of Hipparchus's own coordinates (from palimpsests or other witnesses) to show for a substantial sample of stars whether Ptolemy's entries equal Hipparchan values shifted by 2°40′ in longitude, or differ in ways that require independent measurement; or a pre-registered statistical analysis of the whole catalogue, using modern astrometry, that discriminates between the two hypotheses for defined subsets of stars.
approach: The statistical case has been argued many times, from Vogt (1925) and Newton (1977) through Evans (1987), Graßhoff (1990), Shevchenko (1990) and Dambis and Efremov (2000), with Duke (2002) questioning whether proper motions can separate the two epochs at all. Verbunt and van Gent (2012) already provide a machine-readable catalogue, and Toomer (1984) the standard translation, so teams need not start from the text.

Rebuild the competing tests on one shared footing: a single edition of the catalogue, with variants from Greek witnesses such as Vat. gr. 1594 and the Arabic and Latin tradition inventoried by Ptolemaeus Arabus et Latinus, matched star by star to modern positions from Hipparcos and Gaia DR3, described by Vallenari (2023) for the Gaia Collaboration. The identification of each ancient star with a modern one is the decision that most shapes the data, and doubtful identifications should be flagged rather than silently resolved.

With every assumption explicit, the main hypotheses can be tested side by side: that Ptolemy observed with a miscalibrated instrument, as Evans (1987) proposed; that he adapted Hipparchan coordinates by adding precession; or that the catalogue is a mixture. Reporting results by constellation, magnitude and source subset would show whether different parts of the catalogue have different origins.

The Hipparchan coordinates recovered by Gysembergh, Williams and Zingg (2022) from the Codex Climaci Rescriptus give, for the first time, a direct sample to compare with Ptolemy's entries. Even a few dozen stars, compared after converting between Hipparchus's equatorial and Ptolemy's ecliptic systems, would test the copying hypothesis more directly than error statistics can.

For much of the catalogue the answer is likely to remain probabilistic, with some regions attributable to Hipparchus and others uncertain. Historians of astronomy and astronomers should review both the star identifications and the modelling of proper motion and refraction.

Further direct evidence depends on multispectral imaging of the remaining undertext of the Codex Climaci Rescriptus and other Sinai palimpsests by imaging scientists, and on the Museum of the Bible, St Catherine's Monastery and partner libraries continuing to open these manuscripts to study.

title: Where was the land of Punt?
short: Egypt traded by sea with Punt for over a thousand years, for incense, ebony, gold and baboons, but whether it lay in Africa, Arabia or both remains disputed.
matters: Punt is the best-documented long-distance partner of pharaonic Egypt, attested from the Fifth Dynasty (Sahure) to Ramesses III, and its position determines the scale of Bronze Age Red Sea navigation and the reach of Egyptian exchange into the Horn of Africa or southern Arabia. It bears on the origins of the incense trade, on the early history of the Gash Delta and Eritrean lowland cultures that some archaeologists identify as Puntite, and on how far the Deir el-Bahari reliefs of Hatshepsut record observed people, houses, animals and plants rather than a stylized exotic land.
stuck: Egyptian texts name Punt and its products but give no distances or coastlines, and Punt itself left no texts that name it. The commodities (myrrh and frankincense, ebony, gold, baboons, leopard skins) occur on both sides of the southern Red Sea, so lists and images can be read either way, and proposals have ranged from coastal Sudan and Eritrea to Somalia and western Arabia. Archaeology of the second millennium BCE on both coasts is thin, and harbour finds at Mersa/Wadi Gawasis document Egyptian departure and return rather than the destination.
solved: Independent provenance results for several classes of Punt imports (baboons, aromatic resins, obsidian, ebony, pottery) excavated in dated Egyptian contexts converge on a bounded region, and that region contains contemporary sites whose material culture matches the Puntite goods and ceramics found at Mersa/Wadi Gawasis.
approach: Compile every Egyptian attestation of Punt and Puntites, with commodities, dates, routes and accompanying images, from published corpora and the Deir el-Bahari and Sahure reliefs, and tag each product with its known natural range on both coasts.

Assemble the isotope, ancient DNA and geochemical provenance results now published for baboons, obsidian and resins into one geographic dataset, and map where the evidence overlaps and where it has been inferred from a single specimen.
Identify museum objects likely to be Punt imports in datable contexts (New Kingdom baboon mummies, resin residues, ebony, obsidian from Mersa/Wadi Gawasis) that have not yet been sampled.

Collaborate with primatologists and isotope geochemists to extend oxygen and strontium baselines and mitochondrial reference data for baboons in Eritrea, Sudan, Somalia and Yemen, and with organic chemists on residue analysis of resins against modern Boswellia and Commiphora reference samples.
Test the result against field data from Eritrean, Sudanese and Yemeni coastal sites of the second millennium BCE.

title: How literate was the population of late imperial China?
short: Rawski's 1979 estimate of 30–45 percent male literacy in Qing China has never been tested against a systematic count of signatures and marks on contracts.
matters: Literacy levels underpin arguments about Qing commercial capacity, the reach of print and vernacular fiction, popular religion and sectarian movements, and the state's ability to govern through written documents. Comparative economic history uses Chinese human capital in debates over the Great Divergence, and the claim that the character script did not hold back mass literacy rests largely on Rawski's figures. Estimates of women's literacy shape histories of gender and household management.
stuck: Rawski's range (roughly 30–45 percent of men and 2–10 percent of women with some reading ability) was inferred from school provision, the price and circulation of primers, and observers' impressions rather than from a direct measure. Literacy in China was graded and functional, so a single threshold is hard to define, and scholars since have favoured qualitative studies of 'literacies' over counts. Contracts survive in the hundreds of thousands, but most were written by scribes (daibi) and bear marks, crosses or signatures whose meaning has not been coded systematically, and the published facsimile series are scattered across regions with very different social structures.
solved: A coded sample of at least several thousand Qing contracts from more than one region, recording for each named party and witness whether they wrote their own name, wrote it in a different hand from the scribe, or made a mark, with the proportion of autograph signatures reported by decade, region, sex and role, and an explicit argument for how that proportion relates to reading ability.
approach: The estimates in Rawski (1979) rest on schools, primers and testimony rather than on direct measurement, and the critique in Cohen (1980) and the graded view of literacy in Johnson (1985) left the figures open. Contracts offer a direct measure of a kind Cressy (1980) used for England, and recent work on the Qingshui River manuscripts by Qu (2021) and on everyday genres of writing by Liu (2024) shows how much of that documentation survives.

Before counting anything, the coding rules have to fit Chinese practice. Scribes (daibi) usually wrote every party's name, so a name in the text says little; what matters is whether a party added an autograph signature, a hua ya mark, a cross or a fingerprint, and whether the document names its scribe. Qu (2024) shows that scribes composed rather than copied, which argues for treating scribe identity as a variable in its own right.

Teams could then work through the published facsimile series, starting with the Huizhou documents, the Qingshui River manuscripts and the Taiwan land deeds searchable in the Taiwan History Digital Library, locating each signature block and recording the form of each party's subscription and the scribe's name. Historians and palaeographers would check a random subsample by eye and settle the ambiguous cases.

Linking scribes across documents would be useful even without a literacy rate: it would show how many villages depended on a handful of writers, how that changed over time, and whether some parties signed in their own hand in one deed and by mark in another.

Two readings of the results will need to be kept apart. A low share of autograph signatures might mean low literacy, or a convention that parties marked even when they could write; comparing account books, letters and zazi primers from the same families, as Wen Haibo and Liu Yonghua have proposed, could tell these apart. Any rate will remain a range by region, gender and decade, and it should be set against the age-heaping evidence in Baten (2010).

Progress depends on access. Many contract holdings in county archives and university collections are catalogued but not imaged, and imaged collections are often not public, so the work needs partnerships with the Institute of History in Beijing, the Shanghai Jiao Tong collection, the Guizhou county archives and the Institute of Taiwan History.

title: When was the consonantal text of the Qurʾān standardized?
short: Islamic tradition credits the caliph ʿUthmān (c. 650); some scholars place closure under ʿAbd al-Malik and al-Ḥajjāj (c. 700) or later. Manuscript evidence is now testing these positions.
matters: The date at which the consonantal skeleton (rasm) was fixed determines how far the text can be used as evidence for the first decades of Islam, how its relation to Muhammad's preaching is assessed, and how the early caliphate's religious authority is understood. A mid-seventh-century closure supports reading the Qurʾān as a near-contemporary witness; a Marwanid or later closure would allow for substantial editorial shaping during the conquest period. The question also bears on the history of Arabic orthography and on the reliability of the Islamic tradition's accounts of collection.
stuck: The earliest manuscripts are fragmentary, undated, dispersed across collections and often published only in part, and the Sanaa lower text survives as an erased palimpsest. Radiocarbon dates give the death of the animal whose skin became parchment, not the date of writing, and their ranges often span several decades on either side of 650 and 700. The literary accounts of ʿUthmān's and al-Ḥajjāj's interventions were recorded later and are read differently by scholars with different views of the tradition's reliability.
solved: A published stemmatic analysis of all variants in the dated and datable manuscripts (including the Sanaa lower text and the regional-codex variants), using shared orthographic errors to test whether the surviving Uthmanic-type manuscripts descend from a single written archetype, combined with a radiocarbon and palaeographic model that bounds when that archetype was produced, with results reproducible from open data.
approach: The manuscript work of Déroche (2009), Déroche (2014) and Cellard (2018), the studies of the Sanaa lower text by Sadeghi (2010), Sadeghi (2012) and Hilali (2017), and the stemmatic arguments of Cook (2004), van Putten (2019) and Sidky (2020) already supply most of the method. The open question is how their results combine with the radiocarbon dates and with the later dating defended by Wansbrough (1977) and Shoemaker (2022).

Transcriptions of early manuscripts from Corpus Coranicum and published editions can be aligned verse by verse, with each difference coded as orthographic (spelling conventions, scriptio defectiva), consonantal or a matter of verse division. Keeping these categories separate matters, since shared orthographic idiosyncrasies are the evidence van Putten (2019) used for a single written archetype.

Phylogenetic and stemmatic methods, of the kind Sidky (2020) applied and Fedeli (2020) has discussed for digital editions, can then test rival models: a single Uthmanic archetype copied into regional exemplars, several independent sources later merged, or a text still fluid until the Marwanid reforms. Each predicts a different pattern of shared errors and spelling conventions across manuscripts of different regions and dates.

A tested stemma of the Uthmanic manuscripts, with the regional variants reported in the literary tradition mapped onto it, would be useful in its own right, whatever the date of closure. The Sanaa lower text would sit outside it as a check on how a non-Uthmanic tradition behaves.

Linking the same dataset to radiocarbon results (Marx 2019), palaeographic classes and the Mingana Collection and Tübingen dates would test whether manuscripts placed early by the stemma are also early by carbon. Given calibration ranges and the interval between preparing parchment and writing on it, as Shoemaker (2022) stresses, the date of standardization will probably stay a range of decades, though one that might exclude some positions argued by Sinai (2014) and his critics.

All of this depends on custodians and laboratories: publication and imaging of fragments held at Dār al-Makhṭūṭāt in Sanaa and elsewhere, multispectral imaging of palimpsests, and further radiocarbon dating. Specialists in Qurʾānic manuscripts would need to review every alignment and variant classification.

title: How large was the Roman citizen population in the late Republic and under Augustus?
short: Roman census totals jump from about 910,000 in 70/69 BCE to 4,063,000 in 28 BCE; whether this reflects a change in who was counted or real growth remains disputed.
matters: Estimates of Italy's population under Augustus range from roughly 5–7 million on the low count to 14 million or more on the high count, and every account of late Republican agrarian crisis, slavery, military recruitment, urbanization, colonization and per-capita income in Roman Italy builds on one of them. The low count implies a stagnant or declining free rural population consistent with the Gracchan narrative of peasant displacement; the high count implies substantial growth and a densely settled countryside. The figures are also a benchmark for population estimates of the whole empire.
stuck: The surviving totals are bare numbers transmitted by literary sources (Livy's Periochae, Phlegon of Tralles, Augustus' Res Gestae) with no statement of who was registered, and the text tradition itself varies (the Periocha for 70/69 BCE is transmitted as 900,000, Phlegon gives 910,000, and the Greek version of the Res Gestae differs from the Latin for 28 BCE). The 70/69 BCE figure is widely thought to be an undercount after the Social War enfranchisement, so the size of the jump is itself uncertain. Survey archaeology, the main independent check, depends on site-recovery rates, dating of surface ceramics and assumptions about household size that are hard to calibrate.
solved: A model that converts each reading (low, middle, high) into predicted densities of occupied rural sites and urban areas for specific surveyed regions, compared against harmonized survey datasets with stated recovery rates, showing that one reading fits the observed settlement record within its uncertainty and the others do not.
approach: The debate is mature. Beloch (1886) and Brunt (1971) defended the low count, Frank (1924) and Lo Cascio (1994) the high count, and Hin (2008) a middle reading, while Scheidel (2008) set out what each implies. Later work by de Ligt (2012) and Hin (2013) carried the low and middle counts further, and Launaro (2011) and Witcher (2005) brought field survey into the argument.

The literary side can be gathered into one dataset: every census figure with its textual variants, from Augustus' Res Gestae to the Periocha for 70/69 BCE, together with enfranchisement, colonization and recruitment data and the demographic assumptions of each model. Making those assumptions explicit would show which disagreements are about evidence and which about modelling choices.

Survey data are harder. Published gazetteers from the Tiber Valley (Patterson 2020), the Roman Suburbium, the Pontine Region, the Albegna valley, the Biferno and others would need harmonizing into site counts by period and size class, building on the integration already done by Attema (2022). The decisions that shape the data are how to treat sites dated only broadly and how to compare surveys of different intensity, and specialists who ran the surveys should review them.

With overlapping surveys of different intensity, recovery rates can be estimated rather than assumed, for instance with Bayesian models. That matters because Witcher (2005) showed that the high count requires low recovery, and Fentress (2009) found Albegna densities hard to reconcile with large rural populations.

Scoring the low, middle and high counts against the same evidence would then show which survives. A defensible regional estimate of rural population for Rome's hinterland, with its uncertainty, would be useful even if Italy as a whole stays open, and the national figure will almost certainly remain a range.

Progress needs digitization of legacy survey archives, including the site cards of the South Etruria Survey at the British School at Rome and records held by Italian and Dutch institutions, done in collaboration with archivists and survey directors.

title: Was rongorongo an independent invention of writing?
short: The undeciphered glyphs carved on about two dozen wooden objects from Rapa Nui may be a pre-contact invention of writing or a nineteenth-century response to European literacy.
matters: Writing is generally held to have been invented independently only a handful of times (Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, Mesoamerica), so a pre-contact Rapa Nui script would add a case from a small, isolated island society without cities or bureaucratic states. That would bear on theories that tie writing to administration and urbanism and on what Polynesian societies could develop in isolation. If instead the script arose after the Spanish annexation ceremony of 1770, when islanders were asked to mark a document, it would be a well-documented case of stimulus diffusion, and the question of whether the glyphs encode language at all would remain separate.
stuck: The corpus is small (fewer than 30 objects, about 15,000 glyphs in standard counts), the script ceased to be used in the 1860s after slave raids and epidemics, and nineteenth-century attempts to elicit readings from islanders produced unreliable results. Radiocarbon dates on the wood give only a terminus post quem for carving: most dated objects fall in the late eighteenth or nineteenth century, and the one fifteenth-century result (Tablet D, Échancrée) comes from non-native wood that could have been carved long after it was felled or arrived. Whether the glyphs record speech is itself disputed; claims of logosyllabic structure (Davletshin) and of a lunar calendar on Mamari (Guy) have not been converted into an agreed decipherment, and statistical tests of 'language-likeness' have been shown to misclassify non-linguistic symbol systems.
solved: Direct dates on residues or carving-associated material, or on wood from additional inscribed objects, that securely place glyph carving before 1722, combined with a reading of sign sequences that predicts Rapa Nui words or parallel passages in unseen text and outperforms matched non-linguistic controls.
approach: Compile a single, versioned digital corpus from Barthel's transcription and the newer 3D models and transcriptions (Lastilla et al.; Horley), with explicit sign-list choices recorded so that results can be rerun under alternative segmentations.

Use research agents to run statistical comparisons of rongorongo sequences against both written languages and non-linguistic symbol systems (heraldry, genealogical tallies, Polynesian tattoo and rock-art motif sequences), following Sproat's warnings about such tests, and report which conclusions survive changes in sign classification.
Test proposed readings (the Mamari lunar sequence, numeral and phonetic-complement hypotheses, parallel passages across tablets) by predicting held-out passages rather than by fitting known ones.

Extend radiocarbon and wood identification to the remaining tablets in Washington, St Petersburg, Santiago, London, Berlin and elsewhere, ideally on minimally invasive samples from carved surfaces or associated residues; this requires collaboration with the holding museums, wood anatomists and AMS radiocarbon laboratories.

title: Were Moses Shapira's Deuteronomy fragments an ancient text or an 1880s forgery?
short: Leather strips offered to Berlin and the British Museum in 1883 were dismissed as forgeries and then lost; since 2021 scholars have again argued they preserved a pre-biblical text.
matters: If the fragments were genuine, they would be by far the oldest biblical manuscript known and, on Idan Dershowitz's reading, direct evidence for a source of Deuteronomy, bearing on the composition history of the Pentateuch that critical scholarship has reconstructed only by inference. If they were forged, they are an unusually revealing case of how a nineteenth-century forger anticipated what scholars expected an ancient Hebrew text to look like, alongside the 'Moabite' pottery Shapira had sold to Berlin. The case also tests how scholarly communities judge authenticity when the object itself is lost and only copies and testimony remain.
stuck: The strips were sold at auction in 1885 and have not been traced, so no material analysis is possible. The surviving evidence consists of transcriptions, drawings and printed facsimiles of uneven accuracy, made in 1883 by Shapira, Christian David Ginsburg and others, together with expert verdicts reached in days under poor conditions. Arguments on both sides depend on whether features of the text (letter forms modelled on the Mesha stele, orthography, a variant Decalogue, a structure resembling source-critical reconstructions of Deuteronomy) are read as marks of antiquity or of a forger working from scholarship available in the 1870s.
solved: A published inventory of every linguistic, orthographic, palaeographic and textual feature in the surviving transcriptions, each classed as either attested in sources available by 1883 or first attested in material discovered later (the Dead Sea Scrolls, later Iron Age inscriptions). The question is settled for practical purposes if a set of features unavailable to an 1883 forger proves to be present, or if every feature can be traced to identifiable 1870s models.
approach: Locate, image and transcribe all surviving copies of the text: Ginsburg's papers in British Library Add MS 41294, the Shapira transcription pages Dershowitz found in the Berlin State Library, the 1883 lithographs and newspaper facsimiles, and Clermont-Ganneau's published drawings, and align them as variant witnesses.

Build a reference corpus of what a forger could have known in 1883 (the Mesha stele and its published facsimiles, the Siloam inscription, Gesenius-era grammars, the Hebrew Bible and Samaritan Pentateuch editions, source-critical studies of Deuteronomy by 1883) and test each feature of the text against it.

Compare the same features against post-1947 evidence, chiefly Qumran manuscripts of Deuteronomy and paleo-Hebrew scrolls and later Iron Age inscriptions, flagging any agreement the 1883 corpus cannot explain.

Treat the Berlin committee's report, Ginsburg's reports to the British Museum and Clermont-Ganneau's notes as testimony to be weighed, with dates, conditions of examination and what each examiner actually saw.
High-resolution digitization of British Library Add MS 41294 and the Berlin Shapira inventory, in collaboration with those libraries, is the prerequisite for a reliable critical text.

title: How much American silver reached China between 1550 and 1800?
short: Estimates of the share of Spanish American silver that ended up in China vary widely because mint, shipping and Chinese monetary records have never been reconciled in one account.
matters: The volume of silver entering China is central to the argument that world trade became global after the founding of Manila in 1571, to explanations of the Ming fiscal shift to silver, and to debates over whether a contraction of silver imports helped bring down the Ming in the 1630s–40s. It also bears on European price history, on the Dutch and English East India Companies' balance of trade, and on nineteenth-century arguments that the reversal of silver flows destabilised the Qing.
stuck: Silver reached China by several routes (the Manila galleons, the Cape route via European companies, overland through Central Asia, and from Japan, which was a larger supplier than the Americas for parts of the period), and each route is documented in different archives with different biases. Registered mint and treasury output understates production because of contraband and unregistered silver, and smuggling on the Acapulco–Manila route was extensive. Chinese sources record taxes, prices and exchange rates rather than imports, so arrivals must be inferred, and published estimates (Barrett, Flynn and Giráldez, von Glahn, TePaske) rest on different assumptions about leakage, re-export and Japanese supply.
solved: A route-by-route, decade-by-decade mass balance for 1550–1800 in which American registered production plus an explicit contraband estimate equals the sum of silver retained in the Americas, shipped to Europe, re-exported to Asia, and carried across the Pacific, with China's share derived from these flows and checked against Japanese exports and Chinese monetary indicators (silver–copper exchange rates, tax receipts in silver, price levels).
approach: The registered production series of Garner (1988) and TePaske (2010), the global accounting of Barrett (1990) and the import estimates of Atwell (1982), Flynn and Giráldez (1995) and von Glahn (1996) are the base. Kobata (1965) fixed the scale of Japanese supply, and the galleon histories of Bonialian (2014) and Giráldez (2015) document how much of the Pacific trade escaped registration.

Assemble every published figure into one linked dataset, recording route, decade, original unit (pesos, marks or taels), fineness and whether the number is registered or estimated. Converting all of it to tonnes of fine silver with documented assumptions is what makes the routes comparable and exposes double counting where the same silver appears in mint, treasury and shipping series.

For the Pacific route, read the Manila treasury accounts and galleon registers in the AGI, located through Heredia Herrera (1989), against the Ramo Filipinas in the AGN described by Urrutia de Stebelski (1980). A reconciled Acapulco–Manila series for 1571–1815, set beside contemporary complaints about smuggling, would be useful on its own.

Rival readings of the seventeenth century can then be tested directly. Atwell's case for a collapse of imports after the 1630s and von Glahn's reply in the Journal of Economic History predict different decade totals, while Deng (2008) and Flynn and Giráldez (2002) disagree on how large the inflow was relative to the Chinese economy; VOC finding aids for Deshima and the Canton factory records of the East India Company give independent checks on the Japanese and Cape routes.

On the Chinese side, silver–copper exchange rates and provincial prices from the Qing archives, and from 1736 the Qing Grain Price Database, offer a test of timing rather than volume. Palma and Silva (2024), Irigoin (2009) and Lin (2006) frame the eighteenth-century and closing years, but contraband and the overland route through Central Asia mean China's share will remain a range under stated assumptions.

Progress depends on wider imaging of AGI and AGN legajos, on access to Qing memorials through the First Historical Archives, and on economic historians who read Spanish, Dutch and classical Chinese reviewing each series before it enters the totals.

title: How much iron did Song China produce in the eleventh century?
short: Robert Hartwell's estimate of about 125,000 tons of iron in 1078 is widely repeated, but it rests on fiscal records whose relation to total output is disputed.
matters: Hartwell's figure is the main quantitative support for the idea of a Northern Song 'industrial revolution' and for claims that Chinese iron output in 1078 rivalled that of Britain in the late eighteenth century. It is used in world histories, in comparative arguments about the Great Divergence, and in environmental histories of deforestation and the shift from charcoal to coal. If output was much lower, or largely charcoal-fuelled, the narrative of a Song coal-and-iron breakthrough that later stalled needs revision.
stuck: The figure is extrapolated from iron receipts recorded for state monopoly and tax purposes in compilations such as the Song huiyao and Wenxian tongkao, which record what the state collected, not what was produced, and Hartwell's multiplier from receipts to output is an assumption. Donald Wagner argued that these administrative figures cannot be scaled up so simply, and Tim Wright's review of four decades of citation found that the estimate has been repeated far more often than tested. Archaeological evidence for Song ironworks is patchy: few smelting sites have been excavated and published in detail, and slag volumes, furnace capacities and fuel types have not been surveyed systematically.
solved: An output estimate for the 1070s, with explicit error bounds, built from at least two independent lines of evidence (the fiscal record re-read prefecture by prefecture with a stated model of collection rates, and archaeological slag-heap volumes and furnace capacities from surveyed sites), with the two lines agreeing within their stated uncertainties.
approach: Any revision begins with the case Hartwell (1962) and Hartwell (1966) built from receipt lists in the Song huiyao and Wenxian tongkao, and his longer cycle in Hartwell (1967). The critiques in Wagner (2001) and Wagner (2008), the reception history traced by Wright (2007) and the survey of mining by Golas (1999) set out where that reasoning is weakest.

Extract every mention of ironworks (ye, jian, wu), quotas and receipts from the Song huiyao jigao, Xu zizhi tongjian changbian, Wenxian tongkao and Song gazetteers, through Scripta Sinica and the Chinese Text Project, and tie each to a prefecture and date using CHGIS (2016). The decision that shapes the data is how each figure is classed: quota, actual receipt, tax share of private output, or narrative report.

Several models of what the receipts mean then compete. Hartwell's multiplier treats taxed iron as a fixed fraction of private output; a lower reading treats receipts as close to the output of state works, with private production largely unrecorded; a third allows the fraction to vary with collection rules. Figures that shift with changes in administration rather than with regional demand would count against a fixed multiplier.

A prefecture-by-prefecture register of attested Song iron sites, linking documentary references to published site reports, would be useful even if total output stays uncertain, because it shows where production was concentrated and where fieldwork would test the most.

Archaeology gives a second line of evidence. Slag volumes and furnace capacities at districts around Kuangshancun near Handan, in Cizhou, Shanxi and Henan, and at charcoal-fuelled bloomery sites such as Xiacaopu in Fujian, together with fuel tracers of the kind used by Wayman and Wang (2003) and Liu (2019), could bound output and the share smelted with coal. The answer will remain an order-of-magnitude range, but one with stated error bounds.

That second line depends on archaeometallurgists, such as those at the University of Science and Technology Beijing, and on provincial cultural-relics bureaus permitting survey, sampling and radiocarbon dating. Historians of Song fiscal administration need to review how the textual figures are classed.

title: Which volcanoes caused the great unattributed sulfate spikes in polar ice, above all 1809?
short: Several of the largest volcanic sulfate deposits of the last millennium, in 1230, 1286, 1458, 1695 and 1809, have no securely identified source volcano.
matters: Reconstructions of volcanic climate forcing such as eVolv2k assign every bipolar sulfate spike without a known source to the equator, and source latitude, season and plume height change how much sulfur reached the stratosphere and how cooling was distributed between hemispheres. The 1809 event, estimated at roughly 12–19 Tg of stratospheric sulfur, opens the coldest decade of the last several centuries together with Tambora (1815); attributing it affects explanations of the harvest failures, famines and disease of the 1810s. Identifications also anchor ice-core chronologies: a named, historically dated eruption is a fixed point that can test or correct layer counting, as the reassignment of the 1450s signals to 1453 and 1458 showed.
stuck: The polar ice records the sulfate but not its origin, and the glass shards that could fingerprint a source are microscopic, scarce, and sometimes come from more than one eruption in the same layer. Many candidate volcanoes lie in regions (Melanesia, the Kurils, the Andes, island Southeast Asia) with thin written records for the relevant decades, and their deposits are poorly sampled and poorly dated. Documentary searches have tended to start from a favoured volcano and look for confirmation, and some claimed eyewitness reports have been propagated through secondary citations without checking the original source.
solved: Each spike is assigned to a named volcano by a published match between the major-element (and ideally trace-element) chemistry of glass shards in the ice layer and proximal deposits of that volcano, together with at least one dated documentary witness (an eruption report, ashfall, or optical phenomena such as a dimmed sun or abnormal twilights) consistent with the ice-core timing to within a year.
approach: Build a gazetteer-linked index of every documentary report of ashfall, dimmed or discoloured sun, dry fog, red twilights and unexplained explosions for 1228–1232, 1284–1288, 1456–1460, 1693–1697 and 1807–1810, drawing on Chinese local gazetteers (LoGaRT), Korean and Japanese court records and diaries, Arabic chronicles (OpenITI), Spanish colonial correspondence and ships' logs.

Trace every claimed witness back to the original text and edition, record the exact wording, place and date, and flag reports that rest only on secondary citations; keyword hits should be read in context, since terms for haze, halos and aurorae overlap in premodern Chinese and Japanese sources.

Score each candidate volcano listed in the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program against three tests: the timing window implied by the ice cores, the source latitude implied by the ratio of Greenland to Antarctic deposition and by sulfur isotopes, and the documentary evidence from its region.

For the leading candidates, work with tephrochronologists to sample proximal deposits, obtain radiocarbon or dendro-dated ages, and compare their glass chemistry with cryptotephra extracted from the relevant ice layers in Greenland and Antarctic cores.

title: Did Vermeer use a camera obscura or other optical aids?
short: Optical effects, perspective geometry and technical imaging have been read for and against Vermeer's use of a camera obscura, with no documentary evidence either way.
matters: Vermeer is the test case for broader claims that optical projection shaped European naturalism, including the Hockney–Falco thesis, and for how far seventeenth-century Dutch painting drew on contemporary optics in Delft, the city of Leeuwenhoek. The answer bears on how his paintings were made (tracing, transfer or free construction), on attributions and chronology based on technique, and on whether instruments such as the camera obscura were working tools for painters or mainly objects of natural-philosophical interest.
stuck: No document records Vermeer owning or using an optical device, and the 1676 inventory of his household lists none. The visual evidence (halation, differential focus, perspective and scale relationships) is compatible with optical observation but can also be produced by skilled painting, and proponents and critics have relied on different paintings and different reconstructions. Recent technical imaging has shown underpainting and revisions that complicate any model of direct tracing without settling whether projection was used at some stage.
solved: A quantitative model of the geometry, scale and focus effects predicted by specific optical set-ups in a reconstructed studio, tested across all securely attributed paintings and against their underdrawings and pinhole evidence, that either fits significantly better than free-hand construction with a pin-and-string perspective or is shown to add no explanatory power.
approach: The case for optical use runs from Seymour (1964) and Fink (1971) through the room reconstructions of Steadman (2001), the broader claims of Hockney (2001) and the transfer experiments of Jelley (2017). Against it stand the pinholes found by Wadum (1995), the practical objections of Mills (1998) and Stork (2020), while Wheelock (1977), Huerta (2003) and Weber (2023) place Vermeer within Delft optics and natural philosophy.

Build a corpus of securely attributed paintings with their published technical imaging, drawing on Vandivere (2019) for the Girl with a Pearl Earring, the National Gallery of Art studies in Wieseman (2022), the Rijksmuseum scans of The Milkmaid and the Dresden restoration. What counts as secure, and which state of a painting is measured, shapes the result, since Girl with a Flute has been reassigned to the studio and the Dresden room changed when its Cupid was uncovered.
For each painting, record perspective lines, pinhole positions, object sizes and focus gradients with their measurement error, and compare them with simulated projections from reconstructed studios.

Three hypotheses make different predictions. Tracing from a projection implies image scales consistent with a fixed lens and screen across paintings and outlines laid in directly; observation through a camera without tracing implies optical effects without that scale consistency; pin-and-string construction alone implies perspective that fits the pinholes better than any lens model.

An open table of geometry and technical findings per painting would serve chronology and attribution even if the optical question stays open. Alongside it, a search of Delft notarial, guild and Jesuit records, and of inventories through the Frick Art Reference Library, could show how common optical instruments were in Dutch households, though the answer for Vermeer himself may remain a matter of relative likelihood.

This rests on conservation scientists at the Mauritshuis, Rijksmuseum, National Gallery of Art and Dresden releasing full-resolution datasets, on optical engineers building physical reconstructions, and on art historians and conservators reviewing the measurements.

title: What do James Wilkinson's unread coded dispatches to Spanish officials say?
short: Letters between the US Army's senior general and Spanish Louisiana, written in a code keyed to an unidentified printed dictionary, remain partly or wholly unread.
matters: From 1787 James Wilkinson, later the ranking general of the US Army and governor of Louisiana Territory, took a Spanish pension and reported to the governors of Louisiana as Agent 13, so his coded letters are a running record of what Spain was told about Kentucky separatism, the Mississippi navigation question, frontier military dispositions and, later, the Burr affair. Historians have reconstructed this relationship largely from Spanish summaries, the deciphered letters that officials filed with their replies, and Wilkinson's own self-serving later accounts. Reading the undeciphered portions would show what Wilkinson actually offered, whom he named, and how Spanish policy in the Mississippi Valley responded, and it would test claims about other Americans drawn into the Spanish Conspiracy.
stuck: Much of the correspondence uses a two-part code: a numbered table of names and common words, plus page, column and row references to a printed English dictionary that neither side identified in writing and that no modern researcher has located. Chu, Valenti and Knight (2020) found that the scanned material at the Library of Congress uses at least two distinct table systems and dictionary layouts (roughly 29 versus 39 rows per column), so wordbanks from one letter do not transfer cleanly to another. Their language-model decipherment recovered about three quarters of word tokens on a held-out sample, which leaves many proper names and rare words, the content most valuable to historians, uncertain. The photostats are scattered across Spanish-archive reproduction series, and the scans used in that study are not publicly linked.
solved: A specific printed dictionary edition (or editions) is identified whose page, column and row coordinates reproduce a large set of independently known code–word pairs, including pairs withheld from the matching, and a previously unread dispatch is decoded with that key and checked against the archival original and Spanish replies.
approach: Partition the surviving coded letters by system (the table and dictionary layouts that Chu, Valenti and Knight label 1078 and 1096) before any inference, using their public transcriptions and wordbanks as a starting set and holding back a portion of known pairs for testing.

Assemble a list of English dictionaries in print between about 1760 and 1800 (pocket and spelling dictionaries, including the Entick editions associated with the separate 1806 Burr cipher) with page counts and two-column layouts, and test each edition's scanned pages from Eighteenth Century Collections Online, HathiTrust and Internet Archive for exact matches to the known page–column–row anchors, allowing for pagination offsets.

Recover the alphabetic table separately by constraining unknown table numbers between known anchors and enforcing consistency of repeated codes across all letters, and treat personal-name codes as unresolved unless an independent source confirms them.

Locate and image the manuscript pages from which the transcriptions were made, chiefly the Library of Congress photostats of Archivo General de Indias, Papeles de Cuba legajos 2373–2375, and compare against the originals in Seville; this requires collaboration with Library of Congress and AGI staff where reproductions have not been digitized.
Publish the reconstructed key with its test results and a critical edition of at least one dispatch not represented in any contemporary deciphered copy.

title: Where was Yamatai, the realm of Queen Himiko?
short: A third-century Chinese account describes the Wa polity ruled by Himiko, but its itinerary cannot be followed literally and the Kyushu and Nara candidates have been argued since the Edo period.
matters: The 'Account of the Wa' in the Wei zhi, part of Chen Shou's Sanguozhi (late third century), is the earliest substantial description of political organisation in the Japanese archipelago. If Yamatai lay in the Nara basin, a polity centred on the area that later produced the Yamato kings already led a confederation reaching to northern Kyushu by the 230s, and the first great keyhole tombs mark its rulers; if it lay in Kyushu, Yamato kingship arose separately and later, and the Wei zhi describes a regional confederation. The choice shapes accounts of state formation, of the start of the Kofun period, and of how the early chronicles Kojiki and Nihon shoki relate to the Chinese record.
stuck: Read literally, the Wei zhi's directions and travel times place Yamatai in the ocean far south of Kyushu, so every reconstruction emends either the directions (the Kinai reading turns 'south' into 'east') or the distances and order of stages (the Kyushu reading), and both sides can cite internal inconsistencies. No inscription names Yamatai or Himiko. The archaeological markers each side relies on are themselves disputed: the dates of the earliest keyhole tombs depend on radiocarbon calibration and pottery sequences, the triangular-rimmed deity-and-beast mirrors may be Wei gifts or Japanese products, and Hashihaka, the leading candidate for Himiko's tomb, is an Imperial Household Agency mausoleum closed to excavation.
solved: A set of explicitly stated readings of the Wei zhi itinerary (each with its emendations listed), each predicting where a mid-third-century paramount centre and its subordinate polities should lie, scored against the dated distribution of large settlements, mounded tombs, Chinese imports and mirrors across western Japan. The problem is solved if one reading fits the independently dated archaeological pattern much better than all others under every defensible calibration of the dates.
approach: Encode every stage of the Wei zhi itinerary and the list of subordinate countries in alternative readings (successive versus radial travel from Ito, emended directions, variant units for li and days) and compute the candidate regions each reading predicts.

Build a georeferenced database of Yayoi to early Kofun sites from the Nara National Research Institute's nationwide site-report archive: moated settlements, mounded tombs, Chinese mirrors and coins, iron, and Kibi- and Tōkai-style pottery, each with its stated date basis.

Re-model the absolute dates of the transition to the Kofun period in a single Bayesian framework that combines the Rekihaku and Makimuku radiocarbon series with dendrochronology and pottery phasing, reporting how the Hashihaka date moves under alternative calibration curves and reservoir assumptions.
Test each itinerary reading against this dated distribution and publish the scoring code so that proponents of either theory can substitute their own assumptions.

Narrowing the dates further requires collaboration with radiocarbon and dendrochronology laboratories on new short-lived samples from securely stratified contexts at Makimuku, Yoshinogari and the early Kofun mounds, and with the Imperial Household Agency for any further sampling at Hashihaka.

existing.title: The Emergence of Japanese Kingship

existing.title: Mirrors on Ancient Yamato: The Kurozuka Kofun Discovery and the Question of Yamatai

existing.title: Problems of the Triangular-rimmed Bronze Mirrors with Divinity and Animal Design Unearthed from Japan
existing.note: Argued that these mirrors, unknown in China, were made in Japan by immigrant craftsmen from Wu rather than given by the Wei court, undercutting their use as markers of Himiko's diplomacy.

existing.title: State Formation in Japan: Emergence of a 4th-Century Ruling Elite

existing.title: Himiko and Japan's Elusive Chiefdom of Yamatai: Archaeology, History, and Mythology
existing.note: Fullest English treatment, with a translation of the Wei zhi text, a history of the Japanese debate, and a chapter on Makimuku and the location of Yamatai.

existing.authors: Harunari Hideji, Kobayashi Ken'ichi, Sakamoto Minoru, Imamura Mineo et al.

existing.title: The Archaeology of Japan: From the Earliest Rice Farming Villages to the Rise of the State

title: In what year did the Zhou conquer the Shang?
short: More than forty proposed dates for King Wu's victory over the last Shang king span over a century, and the official choice of 1046 BCE remains disputed.
matters: The conquest year is the pivot of early Chinese absolute chronology: the reign lengths of the Western Zhou kings are counted forward from it, and the late Shang kings, including the oracle-bone reigns at Anyang, are counted back from it. The dates of hundreds of inscribed bronzes, the calendar reconstructions they depend on, and every attempt to synchronize early China with other Bronze Age societies inherit whatever error it carries. Since 841 BCE is the earliest year fixed by continuous Chinese annalistic records, the choice of conquest year also determines how much of the preceding two centuries can be treated as dated history.
stuck: Each line of evidence fixes a date only under assumptions that the others cannot independently check: the 'current' and 'ancient' texts of the Bamboo Annals disagree with each other and with Han reckonings, the five-planet conjunction of 1059 BCE dates a portent rather than the battle, and bronze date formulas such as those on the Li gui can be fitted to many calendars depending on how lunar-phase terms are defined. Radiocarbon dates from Fengxi and Yinxu bracket the transition only to within a few decades. The Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project (preliminary report 2000, final report 2022) chose 1046 BCE by combining these sources, but critics argued that its weighting of evidence was not transparent and that later bronze discoveries contradict its Western Zhou reign scheme.
solved: A published, reproducible model that takes every dated line of evidence as an explicit likelihood (textual reign counts, astronomical retrodictions, bronze calendar data, eclipse records, calibrated radiocarbon), returns a posterior distribution for the conquest year, and reports how that distribution shifts when each contested assumption (text version, lunar-phase definition, identification of an eclipse) is changed. The answer is settled to the extent that defensible alternative assumptions yield overlapping high-probability intervals.
approach: Compile a machine-readable corpus of all Western Zhou bronze inscriptions with full date formulas (year, month, lunar-phase term, ganzhi day) from the Academia Sinica bronze database and recent excavation reports, recording king attributions as uncertain variables.

Encode the rival interpretations of the lunar-phase terms (the four-quarters model versus Liu Xin's fixed-day model and Nivison and Shaughnessy's alternatives) and test each against the full inscription set by computing how many inscriptions each calendar can accommodate.

Retrodict the astronomical claims (the 1059 BCE conjunction, the Jupiter position implied by the Li gui and Guoyu, Shang lunar eclipses in oracle-bone inscriptions) with modern ephemerides, including uncertainty in Delta-T.

Combine these with the Bamboo Annals reign counts and the Fengxi and Yinxu radiocarbon series in a single Bayesian model (for example in OxCal or Stan), and publish the code with sensitivity runs for each contested input.

Narrowing the radiocarbon component requires collaboration with radiocarbon laboratories on new high-precision, short-lived samples from securely stratified pre- and post-conquest contexts at Fengxi and Yinxu, wiggle-matched where timber is available.

existing.title: The Bamboo Annals and Shang-Chou Chronology
existing.note: Critical assessment of how far the Bamboo Annals could be used to build an absolute chronology for the Shang and Zhou.

existing.title: "New" Evidence on the Zhou Conquest
existing.note: Reassessed the transmitted and epigraphic evidence for the conquest campaign and its calendar.

existing.title: Astronomical Dates in Shang and Western Zhou
existing.note: Identified Bamboo Annals accounts of planetary conjunctions with those of 1576 and 1059 BCE and used the latter to argue for a conquest in 1046 BCE.

existing.title: 1040 as the Date of the Chou Conquest
existing.note: Short argument for 1040 BCE based on Nivison's reconstruction of the Bamboo Annals chronology.

existing.title: The Dates of Western Chou
existing.note: Long reconstruction of Western Zhou reign dates from bronze inscriptions and the Bamboo Annals, the foundation of Nivison's later proposals.

existing.title: The "Current" Bamboo Annals and the Date of the Zhou Conquest of Shang
existing.note: Argued that the much-disparaged 'current' text preserves authentic material and that it supports a conquest in 1045 BCE.

existing.title: Sources of Western Zhou History: Inscribed Bronze Vessels
existing.note: Standard guide to using bronze inscriptions as historical sources, with a full treatment of their date formulas and a proposed absolute chronology.

existing.title: The Bamboo Annals Revisited: Problems of Method in Using the Chronicle as a Source for the Chronology of Early Zhou, Part 1
existing.venue: Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 55 (2): 272–297
existing.note: Methodological critique of how the Bamboo Annals had been emended to yield conquest dates (Part 2 followed in the same volume).

existing.title: The Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project: Methodology and Results
existing.note: English statement by the Project's chief scientist of how textual, astronomical and radiocarbon evidence were combined to reach 1046 BCE.

existing.title: Building the Chronology of Early Chinese History
existing.note: Critique of the Project's methods, arguing that its integration of disparate evidence was neither transparent nor independent of its desired conclusions.

existing.authors: Guo Zhiyu, Liu Kexin, Yuan Sixun et al.
existing.title: AMS Radiocarbon Dating of the Fengxi Site in Shaanxi, China
existing.note: Bayesian calibration of a stratified pre- and post-conquest sequence at the Zhou capital, placing the conquest most probably between about 1060 and 1000 BCE.

existing.title: Chronologies of Ancient China: A Critique of the "Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project"
existing.venue: In Clara Wing-chung Ho (ed.), Windows on the Chinese World. Lanham: Lexington Books, 15–28
existing.note: Critique of the Project's Western Zhou chronology and of its handling of bronze and textual evidence.

existing.title: Astrology and Cosmology in Early China: Conforming Earth to Heaven
existing.note: Places the 1059 BCE conjunction and the Mandate of Heaven ideology at the centre of a broader account of early Chinese astral thought, retaining 1046 BCE.

existing.authors: David S. Nivison (ed. Adam C. Schwartz)
existing.title: The Nivison Annals: Selected Works of David S. Nivison on Early Chinese Chronology, Astronomy, and Historiography
existing.note: Collected papers, including a record of the Nivison–Shaughnessy debate on the Bamboo Annals and Nivison's later arguments for a conquest in the 1040s.

existing.title: The Xia Shang Zhou duandai gongcheng baogao and Its Chronology of the Western Zhou Dynasty
existing.note: Review of the Project's 2022 final report, arguing that bronzes published since 2000 show its Western Zhou absolute chronology to be fundamentally flawed and that the report left it uncorrected.
